claims.text: Format compliance of the confirmatory single-call arms was 97.5-100% under the marking rule as run (D-76 with Deviation 2's repeated-line rule; pre-specified descriptive): Haiku-medium 98.6% (3,155 of 3,200) on chains and 99.7% (3,191 of 3,200) on pieces; Opus-medium and Sonnet-medium 97.5% (78 of 80) on chains and 100% on pieces; Opus-low 98.75% (79 of 80) and 100%. E3 (Test 4) has no format-compliance figure, because its step calls are counted as calls made. Under the rule as run, no Test 1-5 reading turns on the remaining parse failures; the marking rule itself matters for Test 3 (Deviation 2). The large format failures sit in the exploratory thinking-off arm: 18.3% non-compliance on chains, the only Study 1 arm whose format flag fires.

Test 4 (Study 1, confirmatory, chains; unadjusted three-way reading): script-split step voting (E3: a script asks each step separately, re-asking until one answer leads by 2 votes, at most 9 calls per step) was worse than one Opus-medium answer by more than the 10-point margin, d = -42.5 [-53.75, -30.0]. E3 scored 53.75 [42.5, 63.75] against 96.25; error ratio 12.33 [5.17, unbounded]. E3 is not an equal-money arm. It cost $0.00356 per puzzle against Opus-medium's $0.0402 (8.8%, about 1/11) and averaged 2.26 draws per step (1,086 draws over 480 steps), so it is a cheap decomposition baseline. The script can split the work for free only because each puzzle lists its steps. No E3 was run at Opus's budget, and one cannot be rebuilt offline because the draws stopped early. Descriptively, E3 scored about 10 points above one Haiku-medium try (53.75 vs 43.72).

claims.text: In Study 1, the Holm correction (used because five tests were run together) declared only Test 5. Holm took the tests in the order 5, 3, 4, 2, 1 and stopped at Test 3 (p = 0.989, above its threshold of 0.00625). The 'worse by more than the margin' readings for Tests 1-4 come from the pre-registered three-way rule on unadjusted two-sided 95% intervals. Their upper ends are -23.75 (Test 1), -26.96 (Test 2), -12.20 (Test 3) and -30.0 (Test 4), against the -10 margin.

Before the main run, the project's fixed power model was fed the length sweep's measured 6-step chain inputs (Haiku-medium right on 92 of 200 tries; Opus-medium 20 of 20, entered as 0.99). It forecast a probability of 1.000 that Test 2 would be conclusive, all of it on 'worse by more than the margin' (spec Amendment 1, item 4; the spec calls this a forecast, not a result). So Test 2's reading was what the model forecast from measured inputs, and the main run's added value lies in the measured gaps, vote curves and costs.

claims.text: Tests 1-5 were pre-registered at 24 steps (lock 1). Declared Deviation 1 moved them after Pilot 1 showed 24 steps was too hard for Haiku, with N = 6 chosen by a pre-set Haiku-only rule and fixed in lock 3 before any main-run data (Amendment 1). The rule took the length whose pooled median Haiku-medium whole-answer score lay closest to 37.5% within 25-50%; 6 and 8 tied at 0.50, and the tie went to fewer steps. Tests 1-3 were therefore read where Haiku-medium's single try scores about 44-51%. claims.text: Vote curve (Study 1, pre-specified descriptive): Haiku-medium's majority vote rose from 43.72 (1 try) to a peak of 58.75 at 33 tries on chains, and from 51.0 to 66.875 at 40 tries on pieces. Opus-medium scored 96.25 / 100 and Sonnet-medium 80 / 75 (chains / pieces). Within 40 tries the vote stayed below both comparators on both shapes, and item 9d finds no break-even price ratio within 40 samples in any of the four comparator-by-shape cells. Forty votes added about 14-16 points over one try. Per correct answer, the chain vote at 36 tries cost $0.0676 [0.0573, 0.0808], against Opus-medium's $0.0418.
The chain vote curve's fall from 58.75 (33 tries) to 57.5 (40 tries) is 1.25 points, within sampling noise, and at 40 tries each puzzle has only one subset of its 40 tries.

Vote sizes (pre-specified descriptive vote curves; the identity follows from the locked 1/m tie rule): a 2-try vote scores the single-try rate, apart from a small gain when one of the two tries is unreadable, so the first real step comes at 3 tries. Haiku-max at 16 steps (Study 1b), pooled: 92.625 (1 try), 92.87 (2), 97.03 (3), 97.45 (4), 98.30 (5), 98.44 (6); each even size added less than the odd size before it. Study 1's Haiku-max: chains 97.5 at 1 and 2 tries, then 100 at 3; pieces 95.0, 95.4, 98.75. Haiku-medium on chains: 43.72, 44.24, 47.53. Practical note (post hoc): B2's equal-money 6 tries is even; on point estimates it scored 0.14 points above 5 tries for 20% more cost (5 tries has no paired interval).

claims.text: Where the Haiku-medium vote helped and where it lost ground (Study 1). The pre-specified lookup chart (item 20) splits each single-try difficulty bin into thirds by pairwise wrong-try agreement, lowest agreement first, and reports the 40-try vote (the equal-money size is 36 on chains and 40 on pieces). On chains, in the 10-20%, 20-30% and 30-40% bins the lowest-agreement third scored 83.3, 100 and 100 at 40 tries while both higher thirds scored 0; the 40-50% bin gave 100 / 66.7 / 16.7. On pieces the pattern is weaker: 66.7 / 0 / 0 in the 20-30% bin, 100 / 100 / 37.5 in the 40-50% bin, and 0 in every third of the 10-20% and 30-40% bins. Below 10% single-try accuracy the vote scored 0 in every third (16 chain and 8 piece puzzles). Cells hold 1 to 6 puzzles; no test. Post hoc counts from the keep-list C9 rows (puzzles with at least 2 wrong tries), at the equal-money vote size: the vote scored below the puzzle's own single-try rate on 28 of 74 chain puzzles and 22 of 75 piece puzzles, above it on 41 and 49, and equal on 5 and 4. claims.text: Flag R (a pre-specified tuning-bias check, reporting definitions §4) did not fire. When two Haiku-medium tries slipped at the same step from the same input, they wrote the same balances in 89.2% of pairs on general steps [90% CI 83.0, 94.9; 11,972 pairs] and in 66.6% on the rule kinds tuned against Haiku [90% CI 59.4, 73.3; 25,082 pairs]. The flag fires only if the tuned-kind rate is at least twice the general one. That is the tilt it guards against: tuned kinds making Haiku's slips repeat, which would work against the vote. The data lean the other way. Slips on the tuned kinds repeat less per pair, though they supply more agreeing pairs because they slip more often.

claims.text: The pre-registered fairness check (D-67; exploratory, flag-based) did not fire. Its targeting index compares Haiku's slip-rate ratio (targeted rule kinds against general steps) with the same ratio for the comparison models; a value above 1 would mean the targeted kinds hit Haiku harder. It was 0.82, 90% CI [0.43, 1.37]. Targeted kinds were harder than general steps for Haiku (slip-rate ratio 4.03, 90% CI [3.23, 5.10]) and for Sonnet (5.37, 90% CI [3.09, 10.70]). Opus made 0 targeted-kind slips and 1 other slip in 948 placed steps, so, as the spec requires when Opus has too few slips, the comparison pools Opus and Sonnet; 38 of its 39 slips are Sonnet's, so it is in effect Haiku against Sonnet. The house-rule index cannot be assessed (0 exposed slips on the comparison side), and the interval cannot exclude a moderate excess targeting of Haiku (up to about 1.4 times).

When paying for Opus, more effort bought no accuracy gain that these data could detect. In Study 1 (keep-list C10, exploratory), Opus-low minus Opus-medium was +1.25 [-3.75, +7.5] on chains and 0.0 on pieces (both 100), at $0.0037 / $0.0033 less per puzzle (about 7-9%). Opus is near the ceiling, so the data cannot separate 'effort does not help Opus' from 'these puzzles are too easy for Opus'.

claims.text: In paired Study 1 data (keep-list C10, exploratory), Haiku-low scored 4.5 points below Haiku-medium on both shapes (chains -4.5 [-6.91, -2.13]; pieces -4.5 [-7.84, -1.09]) for about 6% lower cost per puzzle. The D-42 rewording check moved Haiku-medium's level by +8.75 [0.0, +17.25]. It ran on Haiku-medium only, so whether a gap of this size between weak settings survives a rewording was not checked.

Haiku with thinking off (exploratory arm; medium effort with thinking disabled) scored 22.0 [16.97, 27.31] on chains and 23.5 [18.8, 28.6] on pieces, against Haiku-medium's 43.72 / 51.0, and saved about 19% / 12.5% of the cost per puzzle. The reply format lists only the value after each step (D-31), so with thinking off Haiku has little room to reason. On chains, 18.3% of its replies also failed the format (the format flag fires); scored on the final answer alone, it reached 28.0 instead of the official 22.0. So, by this arithmetic, format failures account for part of the chain shortfall. The design allows thinking to be disabled on Haiku only (at high effort or below; Opus cannot disable it), so there is no Sonnet or Opus counterpart.

At their own equal-money vote sizes (item 10; exploratory, no Holm, no verdict), the weaker Haiku settings also stayed far below one Opus-medium answer. Haiku-low's vote (39 tries on chains; 40 on pieces, capped from 46) scored 49.375 and 62.5: d -46.875 (95% interval -58.125 to -35.625) and -37.5 (-48.125 to -27.5). Haiku thinking-off's vote (40 tries, capped from 45 and 50) scored 42.75 and 40.0: d -53.5 (-64.375 to -42.0) and -60.0 (-70.0 to -48.75). Turning thinking off saved money per call but raised the cost per correct answer, from $0.0025 to $0.0040 on chains and from $0.0021 to $0.0041 on pieces (list price).

claims.text: Post hoc reading of Study 1 (Haiku-max is an exploratory arm; no paired interval was computed). One Haiku-max try ($0.00441 chains, $0.00407 pieces) costs about as much as 4 Haiku-medium tries ($0.00440; about $0.00437). On the same puzzles, the single Haiku-max try scored 97.5 / 95.0 against 49.36 / about 58.95 for a 4-try Haiku-medium vote. Voting at medium effort added about 15 points for 36-40 tries' worth of money; going from medium to max added 44-54 points for about 4 times the money.

Per-piece view (pre-registered secondary descriptive, D-23, item 7). On the pieces shape, a single Haiku-medium try got 89.5% [87.8, 91.2] of single steps right, at $0.000182 per task (about 1/44 of Opus-medium's $0.00802). Haiku-max got 99.0% [98.3, 99.6] at $0.000678 (about 1/12); Opus-medium and Opus-low got 100%. A 40-vote per piece reached 93.75% [91.5, 95.7] at $0.00729 per task. The whole-answer pieces score is close to the per-piece rate compounded six times (0.895^6 = 0.51 against an observed 51.0; post hoc arithmetic).
claims.tier: pre-registered secondary descriptive (item 7); compounding check post hoc

claims.text: A same-meaning rewording of the prompt (D-42(a): a pre-registered robustness check, outside the confirmatory family) raised Haiku-medium's single-try score by +8.75 points [0.0, +17.25] pooled on 40 fixed puzzles (chains +11.5 [0.0, +23.5]; pieces +6.0 [-5.0, +17.0]). Our results may depend partly on wording: the data fit anything from no change to about +17. The size is comparable to the gain from a vote of 5 to 8 tries on chains (+7.0 at 5 tries, +9.3 at 8; descriptive). It is small beside the gaps in Tests 1, 2 and 4 (33-43 points). Test 3, whose interval's upper end (-12.20) lies closest to the -10 margin, is the most exposed. The rewording was checked only on single Haiku-medium tries, not on votes, and never at max effort. On the 20 chain puzzles, the reworded prompt's replies were 100% format-compliant against 98.5% for main-run samples 1-10 (pooled 100% against 99.25%), so at most about 1.5 of the +11.5-point chain gain could come from format; the rewording also made one rule clause clearer.
claims.tier: pre-registered robustness check (no test); format side descriptive

claims.text: The escalate-to-Opus cascade on Haiku-medium votes (item 9e; a pre-specified exploratory offline simulation). It takes a vote of the first k_c Haiku-medium tries (k_c = 5, 10 or 20); if the winning answer's share of that vote is below a threshold tau, it uses Opus-medium's answer instead. Each threshold was chosen on the odd-numbered base puzzles and scored on the 40 even-numbered ones. At k_c = 10 it saved nothing measurable on chains and traded 7.5 points for a 25% saving on pieces. Chains (tau 0.8): 90.0 vs Opus-medium's 92.5 on the same bases, d -2.5 [-7.5, 0.0], escalating 70% of puzzles, at $0.0408 vs $0.0416 (cost difference -0.0008 [-0.0072, +0.0049], spanning zero). Pieces (tau 0.7): 92.5 vs 100, d -7.5 [-15.0, 0.0], escalating 52.5%, at $0.0366 vs $0.0489 (25% cheaper; cost difference -0.0122 [-0.0195, -0.0047]). At k_c = 5 the accuracy loss was larger (chains -10.0 [-20.0, -2.5]; pieces -12.5 [-22.5, -2.5]). A cascade on Haiku-max tries was not simulated.

Shape (six one-step pieces vs one six-step chain; pre-specified descriptive, keep-list C2, C3, C5). In Study 1 at 6 steps, every arm's pieces-minus-chains interval included zero (Opus-low's and Opus-medium's start at zero): Haiku-medium +7.28 [-1.47, +15.38], Haiku-low +7.28 [-0.94, +15.16], Opus-medium +3.75 [0.0, +8.75], Sonnet-medium -5.0 [-18.75, +8.75] and Haiku-max -2.5 [-6.25, +0.83]. For Tests 1-2, the vote's gap to Opus-medium was not shown to differ between shapes (C5: +4.52 [-9.85, +18.23]). In the length sweep (20 bases each, one try), Sonnet-medium scored higher on chains than on pieces at 4 of 5 lengths (6, 8, 12 and 16 steps). In Study 1b, Haiku-max scored lower on pieces than on chains at 6 steps (94.25 vs 97.25; its gap to Opus-medium was -5.75 on pieces vs -1.5 on chains), but higher on pieces at 12 steps (95.125 vs 90.375) and at 16 steps (93.0 vs 92.25). The shape effect did not keep one direction across sets and lengths.
claims.tier: pre-specified descriptive (C2, C3, C5; length sweep; Study 1b per form)

claims.text: Sonnet's shape order is not a stable pattern (descriptive, untested; cross-set readings). In the length sweep (20 bases per length, one try per puzzle, Deviation 2 marking rule) Sonnet-medium scored higher on chains than on pieces at 4 of 5 lengths; the exception is 4 steps (chains 80, pieces 95). Under the original marking rule, which Deviation 2 replaced after these same Sonnet replies had been seen, the count is 3 of 5 (at 6 steps, chains 70 and pieces 75). On Study 1b's 6-step set (40 bases, one try per item), Sonnet-medium scored 77.5 on chains [61.55, 89.16] and 82.5 on pieces [67.22, 92.66]; Sonnet-low scored the same. In Study 1 (80 bases), Sonnet-medium scored 80.0 on chains and 75.0 on pieces (pieces minus chains -5.0 [-18.75, +8.75]), but Sonnet-low scored 71.25 and 76.25 (+5.0 [-8.75, +18.75]). claims.text: Opus-medium vs Sonnet-medium (item 9h, exploratory, no test): +16.25 [6.25, 26.25] points on chains and +25.0 [16.25, 35.0] on pieces, at 2.73 and 2.99 times the cost, and 2.27 [1.95, 2.59] and 2.24 [1.96, 2.52] times the cost per correct answer. Sonnet here ran one level below its default.

Sonnet-low (Study 1, exploratory arm, item 10; no Holm, no verdict; paired over 80 bases) scored 71.25 on chains and 76.25 on pieces. It was not shown to differ from Sonnet-medium (chains -8.75 [-21.25, +3.75]; pieces +1.25 [-10.0, +12.5]). It scored below Opus-low (chains -26.25 [-36.25, -17.5]; pieces -23.75 [-33.75, -15.0]). Its chain score depends on Deviation 2: 52.5 under the original rule. Low and medium Sonnet were not separated in either study (both 80.0 in Study 1b at 6 steps); Sonnet's large gain came at high, which only Study 1b ran.

All headline accuracy results were measured in Batch. In the 10-puzzle real-time subset (pre-specified descriptive, item 6; no test), accuracy was lower in real time than in Batch for all three models (real time vs Batch): Haiku-medium 0.54 vs 0.58 over 50 calls; Opus-medium 0.9 vs 1.0 and Sonnet-medium 0.7 vs 0.9 over 10 calls each. Output tokens were within about 1-7%. Pilot 1's real-time check (exploratory; 24 steps, 5 base puzzles in both shapes, original marking rule) pointed in mixed directions: Opus-medium chains 100% in real time against 60% in Batch (5 tries each; pieces 100% in both), Sonnet-medium pieces 20% against 40% and chains 40% against 20%, Haiku-medium 0% whole answer in both (79.2% against 81.1% per piece). The subsets are far too small to tell whether there is a real difference in either direction.

Effort diagnostic (exploratory, Haiku only, $0.42; the record behind Deviation 1). On identical prompt text, free Claude Code helpers got 141 of 144 single pieces right (98%), API Haiku-medium 110 of 144 (76%) and API Haiku-high 127 of 144 (88%). High scored above medium on all 6 prompts (if the two were equally good, 6 of 6 would happen by chance 1 time in 64). Claude Code's effort and thinking budget were not recorded, so the gap is unexplained.

The pre-specified low-information flag did not fire: Haiku-medium scored 51.0% on pieces (the flag fires if its single-try score on pieces is above 60%; reporting definitions item 5). Haiku-medium's per-puzzle single-try scores spread to both ends: on chains, 16 of 80 puzzles were below 10% and 11 at 90% or more. The median over puzzles was 40.0 on chains and 50.0 on pieces.

claims.text: B2 (Study 1b, confirmatory; the only primary Study 1b test declared under Holm). On fresh 16-step procedures, the expected accuracy of a 6-try Haiku-max vote (estimated from 10 tries per item) was no worse than one Opus-medium answer by more than 5 points: d +0.63 points, 95% interval -1.15 to +2.44; p = 0.0001, below its Holm threshold of 0.0083. It came at about Opus-medium's price per answer (k = 6 measured; list cost $0.0670 vs $0.0750, ratio 0.894). Per shape, the vote cost 1.091 times Opus-medium's price on chains (more than Opus) and 0.733 on pieces. Accuracy 98.44 vs 97.81; error ratio 0.71 [0.24, 2.11]. The reading is the same in all three views and in the sensitivity check that drops the one base puzzle in B2's set whose answer key appeared in a helper work session (+0.64 [-1.20, +2.50], 79 bases). B2 shows 'no worse by more than 5 points' at about equal money; it is neither a saving nor superiority.

B1 (Study 1b, confirmatory; Holm within Study 1b): at 16 steps we could not show that a single Haiku-max try is within 5 points of Opus-medium (d -5.19 points, 95% interval -7.75 to -2.69; p = 0.566). Its error rate was 3.4 times Opus's (95% interval 1.8 to 10.1). (Descriptive, not a pre-registered test: the whole 95% interval lies below zero.) At the secondary 10-point margin, it was no worse than Opus-medium by more than 10 points (p = 0.00027). One try costs about 1/6 of Opus-medium's per answer (k measured; the measured ratio is 6.71). Accuracy 92.625 vs 97.8125.

claims.text: B3 (Study 1b, confirmatory; 6 steps, 40 bases): we could not show that a single Haiku-max try is within 5 points of Opus-medium (d -3.63, 95% interval -7.0 to -1.5; p = 0.206). Its error rate was 6.8 times Opus's (95% interval 1.7 to unbounded; Opus-medium made 1 error in 160 tries). (Descriptive, not a pre-registered test: the whole interval lies below zero.) At the secondary 10-point margin, it was no worse than Opus-medium by more than 10 points (p = 0.0011). It costs about 1/10 of Opus-medium's per answer (k measured). Accuracy 95.75 vs 99.375.

The pre-registered sensitivity that leaves out the base puzzles whose answer keys appeared in a helper work session (one in the 16-step set, two in the 6-step set; 79, 79 and 38 bases) gives the same readings for all three tests in all three views: B1 d -5.19 (95% interval -7.85 to -2.66), inconclusive at 5 points and no worse than Opus-medium by more than 10 (p = 0.00014); B2 +0.64 (-1.20 to +2.50), no worse by more than 5; B3 -3.82 (-7.50 to -1.45), inconclusive at 5 and no worse by more than 10 (p = 0.0016).

Study 1b's locked power table (spec §5) said in advance that, near Opus's ceiling, a 5-point margin confirms 'no worse' only if Haiku-max's true accuracy is close to Opus's. With Opus at 98% (Holm's strictest step), B1's chance of reading 'no worse by more than 5 points' was 0.89-0.99 if Haiku-max were at 98%, 0.23-0.31 at 95% and 0.00-0.01 at 92%. Haiku-max scored 92.625 at 16 steps, so an inconclusive B1 was the expected outcome for a gap of this size; the error-rate ratio beside the test carries the size of the gap.

claims.text: Opus-medium is at or near the ceiling (96.25-100), so error-rate ratios, not point gaps alone, carry the size of each result: the error ratio sits beside every d. Where an arm made zero errors, the zero-width cluster-bootstrap interval (for example [100, 100]) is replaced with the exact Clopper-Pearson bound (0 errors in 80: 95% upper bound 4.51%). A 10-point margin near a 98% ceiling allows several times Opus's error rate (B1 met it with an error ratio of 3.4).

For Haiku-medium, q is the share of single pieces right on the pieces shape, pooled over the five lengths: q = 0.905 (95% interval 0.893 to 0.918). The dashed line q^N shows what a whole answer would score if every step were an independent piece. claims.text: E2 against E3 on chains is not like for like. It spans two run windows (E3 from the main run, E2 from the top-up). Neither multi-call design decided how to split the task: step voting (E3; C13 on pieces) takes its steps straight from the puzzle, which lists them, and that split costs nothing only because the steps are given; the team's planner was told to write one instruction per listed rule (chains) or per sequence (pieces), labelled Task 1 to Task 6, and a plan without exactly Task 1 to Task 6, each once and none empty, counted the puzzle as wrong (no plan failed on either shape). The helpers voted by E3's lead-by-2, cap-9 rule. By design E2 differs from step voting in three ways: who writes the step instructions; on chains only, helpers start from the team's own agreed result for the previous step rather than the correct inputs; and an aggregator may redo a step. E3's correct-input scoring does not by itself favour E3 under the all-step-lines-right score: the product of per-step accuracies equals the chance that a chain of independent step calls gets every step right (spec, D-68 F7). claims.text: Practical rules (a post hoc synthesis; each step keeps its own tier). (1) For a cheap model, raise thinking to max before paying for a bigger model. The confirmatory part: B1 and B3 were no worse than Opus-medium by more than the secondary 10-point margin, at about 1/6 to 1/10 of the cost per answer, but were not shown within 5 points. (2) Don't try to buy accuracy with many medium-effort cheap calls (Tests 1, 2 and 4, unadjusted three-way readings; the top-up arms are exploratory). (3) If you need accuracy no worse than Opus-medium's by more than 5 points at about its price, vote a few max-effort cheap tries, and work out the equal-money vote size for your own task and shape (B2: 6 Haiku-max tries at 16 steps, 0.894 of Opus's price pooled, but 1.091 on chains and 0.733 on pieces). On that day Batch, at half the list price, returned whole waves in about 2 to 16 minutes. The waves mixed all of Study 1's single-call arms, Haiku-max's 480 calls among them, so no per-arm turnaround exists. Study 1b's and the top-up's analysis files report no turnaround.

Every Batch-run arm was billed at exactly half its list price (item 9b batch_mean = mean / 2; for the six real-time arms batch_mean equals mean), so Batch changes the dollars, not the ranking of setups. In the 10-puzzle real-time subset, output tokens per call were close to Batch (Haiku 1,791 vs 1,813), and real time cost 1.87-1.99 times Batch on the same puzzles. Before Study 1b, $35.74 of $41.73 (86%) went through Batch; Study 1b and the top-up were Batch only, so about 94% of the $104.16 spent overall went through Batch (post hoc arithmetic).

claims.text: Scope: one synthetic exact-answer ledger task family (ledger-0.5, l14 rules, 4-16 steps; its rule kinds were developed in free Claude Code helper checks with Haiku 5.5 alone, effort unrecorded, adding kinds where Haiku slipped); Claude 5.5 models only (Fable 5.1 dropped, D-27); short prompts (about 1,000-1,900 input tokens); temperature fixed at the API default of 1; Batch execution; list prices of 2026-10-12/13. Haiku's over-100K-input price tier would cut Opus's price ratio from 40 times to 8 times, so long-context and agent work need their own measurement.

claims.text: Main message (a post hoc synthesis; each part keeps its own tier): effort first, then voting. On one synthetic family of exact multi-step puzzles, raising Haiku 5.5's effort to max helped far more than any multi-call design tried at medium effort. At no more than Opus-medium's price, medium-effort Haiku votes were worse than one Opus-medium answer by more than the 10-point margin (Tests 1-2, unadjusted three-way readings), and so was step voting, at about 1/11 of the cost (Test 4). The Haiku team stayed 27.5-43.75 points below Opus-medium, and the Haiku picker's 62.5 / 67.5 sat about 33 points below Opus-medium's 96.25 / 100 (both exploratory; the picker gap is arithmetic, with no interval). A single Haiku-max try, at about 1/6 to 1/10 of the cost per answer, could not be shown within 5 points of Opus-medium (B1, B3), but was no worse than it by more than the secondary 10-point margin. At 16 steps, a 6-try Haiku-max vote was no worse than one Opus-medium answer by more than 5 points, at about its price (B2).
claims.tier: post hoc synthesis (each part keeps its own tier)

claims.text: Every comparison between Study 1 and Study 1b (different puzzle sets, days and sample sizes) is descriptive only, never a test. Top-up arms compared with main-run arms are exploratory, cross-window comparisons, each carrying the same-model flag; none is a test. Study 1 and Study 1b are never pooled in one Holm family, and the effort sweep and vote curves are never set beside the tests as evidence. At 6 steps, Study 1 used its main set (80 bases, 2026-10-12) and Study 1b its separate 6-step set (40 bases, 2026-10-13).

claims.text: Two 6-step sets from the same generator gave the weak Haiku arms scores 5-10 points apart (cross-study, descriptive): Haiku-medium 54.5 [46.0, 63.25] on Study 1b's 6-step set vs 47.36 [42.3, 52.6] on Study 1's main set; Haiku-low 52.75 vs 42.86; thinking off 27.5 vs 22.75. Haiku-max (95.75 vs 96.25) and Opus-medium (99.375 vs 98.125) barely moved. The intervals overlap, but the spread is as large as some differences one might read across studies, so every length comparison is taken from one study's sets.

claims.text: Share of errors a vote removed (post hoc arithmetic on stamped points; descriptive, cross-study, no test). Haiku-medium in Study 1: on chains 56.28 error points for one try against 41.39 for the 36-try equal-money vote (about 26% removed); on pieces 49.0 against 33.125 at 40 tries (about 32%). Haiku-max in Study 1b at 16 steps: 7.375 for one try against 1.555 for the 6-try vote (about 79%) and 0.625 at 10 tries (about 92%). Study 1's 3-try Haiku-max vote: chains 2.5 to 0.0, pieces 5.0 to 1.25. The point gain from voting was smaller at max effort (+5.8 to 6 tries) than at medium (+14.9 chains, +15.9 pieces), but the share of errors removed was far larger. This describes the curves; it does not explain them (no Haiku-max repeat share exists).

user_framing_choices.question: How should Test 5's scope be worded, given Sonnet ran one level below its default effort?
user_framing_choices.background: Test 5 compared Opus-low with Sonnet-medium; Sonnet's default is high. On Study 1b's other 6-step puzzles, Sonnet-high scored 97.5 at under half Opus-low's price per answer (descriptive, cross-study).
user_framing_choices.why_it_matters: It decides whether readers see Test 5 as a scoped confirmatory result or as a weakened one.
user_framing_choices.option_a: Say the Study 1b numbers 'bound' Test 5.
user_framing_choices.option_b: Say the Study 1b numbers 'undercut' Test 5.
user_framing_choices.option_merged: No verb either way: beside Test 5, state that Sonnet-medium is one level below Sonnet's default and that Test 5 says nothing about Opus-low against Sonnet at its default effort, then give the labelled cross-study Study 1b numbers.
user_framing_choices.why: Both verbs editorialise. The merged sentence is the checked fact and keeps the confirmatory and cross-study tiers apart.

user_framing_choices.question: How hard should the paper lean on the pre-run power forecast for Test 2?
user_framing_choices.background: Before the main run, the locked power model, fed the length sweep's measured inputs, forecast with probability 1.000 that Test 2 would read 'worse by more than the margin'. The spec calls this a forecast, not a result.
user_framing_choices.why_it_matters: It shapes whether Study 1's value is presented as the tests or as the measured gaps, curves and costs.
user_framing_choices.option_a: Leave it to the methods appendix.
user_framing_choices.option_b: Lead with it: Tests 1-2 'confirmed an expected outcome'.
user_framing_choices.option_merged: One sentence beside Test 2 in Results: the locked power model forecast this reading from measured pilot inputs (a forecast for Test 2 only); details in the appendix.
user_framing_choices.why: It is honest and short. B's version stretches a Test 2 forecast to Tests 1-2 and to certainty.

user_framing_choices.question: How strongly to frame that Tests 1-4 held effort at medium?
user_framing_choices.background: Every confirmatory Study 1 arm was at medium effort. Haiku-max (3 tries) was the only arm above medium and the first extra to trim (D-27). It became a test only in Study 1b.
user_framing_choices.why_it_matters: It sets the story's spine: the surprise the data pointed to, or a design that tested the wrong lever.
user_framing_choices.option_a: A: Haiku-max is the surprise the data pointed to.
user_framing_choices.option_b: B: the medium-only confirmatory family is a design lesson ('wrong lever').
user_framing_choices.option_merged: State the design fact plainly when Study 1b is introduced (row R-09), keep D-125's surprise framing, and do not use 'wrong lever'.
user_framing_choices.why: D-125 already confirmed the Haiku-max result as the surprise the story turns on. Stating the design fact plainly answers B's concern without adding a new frame.

user_framing_choices.question: Where do Deviation 1's 6-step regime and the effort diagnostic go?
user_framing_choices.background: Deviation 1 moved Tests 1-5 from 24 to 6 steps by a Haiku-only rule. The effort diagnostic (Claude Code against the API) is the record behind it.
user_framing_choices.why_it_matters: It sets how much of the journey goes in the main text.
user_framing_choices.option_a: Both in the main-text Results.
user_framing_choices.option_b: Both in the appendix.
user_framing_choices.option_merged: Deviation 1 and the 6-step regime sentence go briefly in the main text where Tests 1-5 are first reported. The effort diagnostic goes in the appendix, with one line in Method. B's untested 'best case for voting' is dropped.
user_framing_choices.why: This follows the team plan under D-121(4) (only the turns that explain the method go in the main text) and the approved style sheet (Deviation 1 travels with Tests 1-5).

user_framing_choices.question: How much of the cheap-judge question does the paper claim to answer?
user_framing_choices.background: The only direct arm is one Haiku-medium picker over 8 Haiku-medium answers, shown in a fixed order. The team's aggregator is an indirect second case. The cheap-judge study itself was dropped earlier.
user_framing_choices.why_it_matters: It is the second question in the project brief, and readers will look for an answer to it.
user_framing_choices.option_a: A: 'the question stays largely open'.
user_framing_choices.option_b: B: list exactly what was not tested.
user_framing_choices.option_merged: Row R-55's text (what was not tested, then 'largely open', no generalising), plus row G2-26's aggregator line as exploratory counts.
user_framing_choices.why: It is honest about the narrow evidence and still reports what was measured.

user_framing_choices.question: Where do the practical buying rules go?
user_framing_choices.background: The rules (raise effort first, do not buy accuracy with many medium calls, vote a few max-effort tries at about equal money) are a post hoc synthesis across tiers.
user_framing_choices.why_it_matters: Practitioners will quote them, so their tier must stay visible.
user_framing_choices.option_a: In Results, each rule labelled.
user_framing_choices.option_b: In the Discussion only.
user_framing_choices.option_merged: The measured facts (R-62 numbers) stay in Results. The rules (R-63) go in a labelled post hoc paragraph in the Discussion, each step carrying its tier, with no frontier.
user_framing_choices.why: Results stay tier-clean, and the rules remain usable.

user_framing_choices.question: The main message paragraph
user_framing_choices.background: The D-116 candidate is 'effort first, then voting'. The user delegated the one sentence to remember to the team (D-121(6)).
user_framing_choices.why_it_matters: It anchors the abstract and the introduction.
user_framing_choices.option_a: A's wording, inside D-116's three parts.
user_framing_choices.option_b: B's wording ('within 2 to 8 points', 'a seventh'), which breaks the wording rules.
user_framing_choices.option_merged: Row R-69's checked text.
user_framing_choices.why: It keeps every part's tier, uses 'k measured' fractions and contains no barred phrase.

user_framing_choices.question: Should costs also be shown per 10,000 puzzles?
user_framing_choices.background: At 6-step chains, list cost per 10,000 puzzles is about $402 for Opus-medium, $147 for Sonnet-medium, $44 for one Haiku-max try and $11 for one Haiku-medium try.
user_framing_choices.why_it_matters: It is easier for readers to picture, but it risks being quoted without the accuracies beside it.
user_framing_choices.option_a: Per-answer dollars only.
user_framing_choices.option_b: Per-10,000-puzzle figures in the text.
user_framing_choices.option_merged: Per-answer list dollars in the tables. One optional per-10,000 sentence in the Discussion, with the accuracies (96.25, 80.0, 97.5, 43.72) and Haiku-max's exploratory label beside it.
user_framing_choices.why: It keeps the reader-friendly figure without letting it stand alone.

must_not_claim: Never 'matches', 'matched', 'as good as', 'level with', 'on par', 'Opus-level', 'can stand in for', 'closed the gap', 'reached Opus's range', 'measurably below' for any result (incl. B2, Test 5, R-47's 5- and 6-try point estimates).
Never call Tests 1-4 'declared' or Holm-controlled; their readings are the unadjusted three-way rule (R-07).
Never say Test 3 holds 'only under Deviation 2'; it also holds in the final-answer and ties-as-wrong views, and is inconclusive under the original rule and copy-slips-forgiven (R-02, R-03).

Never describe B1 or B3 as 'worse', 'measurably/statistically worse' or 'one-seventh of the price'; use the §10 inconclusive template with the error ratio and 'about 1/6 / 1/10 (k measured)' (R-30, R-31).
Never present B2 as a saving or superiority, or say a vote costs 'a fraction of Opus's price'; it is no worse by more than 5 points at about equal money (1.091 on chains) (R-32).
Never say Study 1b 'replicated' Study 1, or that B1-B3 show generality beyond the ledger family (R-20, R-34).
Never read the chain vote dip (58.75 to 57.5) as 'more votes hurt' (R-11).
Never 'voting fails because errors repeat' or any causal claim about the plateau; never 'repetition is only weakly related to difficulty' on chains (R-12, R-13, G2-02).
Never 'voting doesn't work': votes added about 14-16 points at medium effort, and at max effort a 6-try vote was no worse by more than 5 points (R-71).
Never suggest a different temperature would lift the medium-effort vote plateau; temperature is fixed at 1 by the API (G3-03).
Never call vote@3 at 16 steps (45% of Opus's price) a saving; no paired interval exists for k other than 6 (R-47).
Never present Haiku-max votes as the cheapest route to that accuracy among all options at 12-16 steps; Study 1b ran only Opus-medium beside Haiku there (R-48).
Never say Sonnet (any effort) or Opus-low ran only at 6 steps without 'in Study 1b'; the length sweep ran Sonnet-medium at 12 and 16 steps (R-48, R-71, L-20, X-41).
Never say the Haiku-max gap to Opus widens with length (G2-23); quote the cost ratio per length, never as one number (R-43).
Never write 'flat' or 'Opus-high is worse' for the Opus effort points; write '96.25-100, not rising steadily with effort'; Opus-high missed 3 times, not once (R-38, G2-21).
Never 'accuracy follows tokens, not the label' (G2-13); never 'rose with effort in every shape' (G2-29).
Never say the 16-step thinking-off score is mostly a format failure (R-39).

Never word compounding as a finding ('chains compound faster', 'exactly compounded', 'compounding cannot explain it'); never say Sonnet 'does better on chains' in general or that its chains 'beat' what compounding predicts (R-41, R-42, G3-01).
Never compare 'thinking off' across models; only Haiku can disable thinking (G2-17).
Never write 'Claude Code beats the API' (R-29).
Never 'strong position bias' or 'mostly chose sample 1' for the picker (R-53); never 'picking helps on chains, re-working helps on pieces' (G3-06).
Never generalise the picker to LLM-as-judge in general (R-55).
Never say votes were untested at max effort (Study 1's 3 tries and B2 ran) (R-56).
Never 'Test 4 at pieces' in prose while L-22 is open; never call the C13 reading 'confirmed' (R-51).
Never present a Study 1 vs Study 1b or top-up vs main-run comparison as a test or 'confirmed' (R-70).
Never say the 5-try vote latency or Haiku-max latency was measured (R-65, X-39).
Never extend the vote results to other lengths; no equal-money Haiku-medium vote was run outside 6 steps (R-28).
Never 'pre-registered at 6 steps' without Deviation 1 (R-28).
Never claim Test 5 says anything about Sonnet at its default effort, or that it confirms or refutes the vendor's 'cheaper per task' advice in general (R-06, G2-09).
Never apply the 'verbosity tax' refutation beyond medium effort (R-59).
Never choose setups by cost per correct answer alone (R-61).
Never compute a Study 1 'Opus-low vs Sonnet-high' Test 5 analogue; Study 1 ran no Sonnet-high (G2-22).
Never copy the stamped confirmatory.headline_wording strings or test4_pieces.methods_note (R-72, R-58).
disclosures: Tests 1-5 were pre-registered at 24 steps (lock 1) and moved to 6 steps by declared Deviation 1, with N fixed by a Haiku-only rule in lock 3 before any main-run data; say so where Tests 1-5 are first reported (R-28).

Deviation 2 (repeated-line marking rule) was declared before main-run data after Sonnet's length-sweep replies were seen; one original-rule line beside Tests 3 and 5 in the main text, the full original-rule tables in the appendix (D-90; R-03, G1-11).

Study 1b was designed after Study 1's results were opened (margin, vote cap, 16 steps chosen knowing the Haiku-max numbers); its sets were frozen earlier, never sent, never attempted by a free helper (R-34).

Exposed bases: one base in the 16-step set and two in the 6-step set; the pre-registered sensitivity re-ran B1-B3 and their error ratios without them; the descriptive outputs of spec §6 were not re-run without them (R-32, G2-16).
Keep-list analyses (C2, C3, C5, C7, C9, C10) are pre-specified descriptive but were computed after the confirmatory results were opened (groupc.json label).
The top-up ran inside the main run's original 48-hour window by declared change (D-110 to D-112); use Edith's replacement methods text, not the stamped test4_pieces.methods_note (R-58).
All headline accuracies were measured in Batch; headline costs are list prices, twice the Batch price paid (except the 70-call real-time subset) (R-27, R-67, G2-10).
Item 19 thinking-token figures are estimates (visible tokens = characters / 3) (R-60).
The stamped headline_wording strings use barred wording and are translated in the data README, never copied (R-72).

reviewer_risks.risk: Small samples and wide intervals: Study 1 test intervals are 18.75 to 23.92 points wide; Study 1b's 3.59 to 5.5; Sonnet and non-medium Opus effort points rest on one try over 40 bases; the same-model check on 20 bases (18-point interval); the real-time check on 10 puzzles.
reviewer_risks.answer: Power was simulated and locked before the data; beside each check say what it could and could not detect (e.g. drifts under about 10 points), call the Opus-high dip consistent with noise, and never read an order into overlapping effort points (G1-20).

reviewer_risks.risk: Near-ceiling comparator: Opus-medium at 96.25-100 makes point gaps small and some intervals zero-width.
reviewer_risks.answer: Error ratio beside every d; exact Clopper-Pearson bounds replace zero-width bootstrap intervals; the 10-point margin near a 98% ceiling allows several times Opus's error rate, which is why the 5-point margin is primary (R-35, R-33).

reviewer_risks.risk: Test 3 depends on the marking rule.
reviewer_risks.answer: Under the original rule and the copy-slips view Test 3 is inconclusive; it holds as-run, in final-answer and ties-as-wrong views; one original-rule line beside Test 3 in the main text (D-90; R-02, R-03, G1-14).

reviewer_risks.risk: Study 1b was designed after seeing Study 1's Haiku-max numbers (winner's-curse style concern).
reviewer_risks.answer: Separate lock before any Study 1b call; test sets frozen before any Haiku-max data and never sent; same family, so no generality claim; B1 and B3 stayed inconclusive at 5 points, which is what the locked power table expected (R-34, R-33).

reviewer_risks.risk: Did Deviation 1 (24 to 6 steps) create the negative vote result?
reviewer_risks.answer: At 24 steps (Pilot 1) Haiku-medium's single try scored 0.4% on pieces and 1.2% on chains against Opus-medium's 96% and 88%, so a vote would not have come near Opus there either; N = 6 was picked by a Haiku-only rule with the ladder's Opus and Sonnet answers sealed (G2-12).

reviewer_risks.risk: Test 4 scores E3 from correct inputs at each step: an oracle advantage?
reviewer_risks.answer: The product of per-step accuracies on correct inputs equals the chance that a chain of independent step calls gets every step right and is a lower bound on final-answer accuracy (spec D-68 F7); do not cite 'H2 cannot fail on dollars' in Test 4's defence (G2-11).

reviewer_risks.risk: Cross-window comparisons in the top-up.
reviewer_risks.answer: The same-model flag did not fire, but its interval cannot rule out 8-10-point shifts; every cross-window comparison carries the flag status; E2 vs C13 is the same-window comparison (R-57, R-49).

reviewer_risks.risk: Puzzles were tuned on Haiku's slips.
reviewer_risks.answer: Flag R and flag K did not fire; targeting index 0.82 (90% CI 0.43 to 1.37) cannot exclude up to about 1.4x excess targeting; the comparison side is in effect Sonnet only (R-14, R-16, R-68).

tables_figures.title: Study 1 confirmatory tests (Tests 1-5)
tables_figures.content: Rows: Test 1 (pieces, Haiku-medium vote vs Opus-medium), Test 2 (chains, same), Test 3 (chains, Haiku-medium vote vs Sonnet-medium), Test 4 (chains, step voting E3 vs Opus-medium), Test 5 (chains, Opus-low vs Sonnet-medium). claims.text: All results come from one synthetic, procedurally generated task family: ledger puzzles with one exact answer, at 4 to 16 steps in the studies and 24 steps in Pilot 1. Its rule kinds were developed in small free test runs with Claude Haiku 5.5 inside Claude Code, whose effort setting was not recorded. We scope the title, abstract and every claim to exact-answer, multi-step rule-following puzzles of this family, and offer the paper as a careful case study plus a reusable protocol: equal money, effort as an axis, exact marking, public locks and disclosed deviations. A second (code-tracing) family was dropped and the planned ArXivMath check was not run; both are future work.

claims.text: Scope of the setting: Claude 5.5 Haiku, Sonnet and Opus under fixed model IDs that carry no date suffix (Haiku 5.5 released 2026-10-07); list prices checked on 2026-10-12 and re-checked on 2026-10-13; Batch execution (headline costs at list price, twice the Batch price paid); short prompts of about 970 to 1,920 input tokens; temperature fixed at 1 by the API; paid ledger-family runs from 2026-10-11 to 2026-10-13. Haiku's long-prompt tier (over 100,000 input tokens) would cut Opus's per-token price ratio from 40x to 8x, so long-context and agent work need their own measurement. The most expensive model on the price list, Fable 5.1 ($10 / $50 per million tokens), was not included.

claims.text: Every try was drawn at temperature 1: on all four models the project checked (Haiku, Sonnet and Opus 5.5, and Fable 5.1) any other temperature, any top_k and any top_p other than 0.99 return an API error. How alike Haiku's tries are is therefore a property of the model under this API, not a setting we chose, and we do not suggest that another temperature would lift the medium-effort vote plateau.

A same-meaning rewording of the prompt's opening and closing paragraphs (a robustness arm ruled in the plan; its comparison fixed after lock 3 and before any result was opened; outside the confirmatory family; no test) moved Haiku-medium by +8.75 points pooled (95% interval 0.0 to +17.25; chains +11.5, 0.0 to +23.5; pieces +6.0, -5.0 to +17.0; 20 bases x 2 shapes, 10 tries each). Format explains at most about 1.5 points of the chain gain (reworded replies 100% format-compliant against 98.5%). Haiku-medium's score may depend partly on wording; the pooled shift is about the gain of a 4- to 7-try vote, far below the 24.7 to 42.5-point gaps in Tests 1-4. It was never checked at max effort.

claims.text: Tuning bias runs both ways. The rule kinds were developed on Haiku's slips, which works against the Haiku vote; other choices work for it: the 10-point margin, refusals and truncations counted as wrong, and a 25-50% difficulty band where voting helps most. In the plan's words, 'the net direction is not known in advance'. The pre-registered fairness check (exploratory, flag-based) gave a targeting index of 0.82 (90% interval 0.43 to 1.37; 1 means no extra targeting), and its flag did not fire; but Opus-medium slipped once in 948 placed steps, so the comparison side is in effect Sonnet, the house-rule index could not be assessed, and the interval cannot exclude the tuned kinds targeting Haiku up to about 37% more than the comparison models. A second pre-registered check (flag R) did not fire: when two Haiku-medium tries slipped at the same step from the same input, they wrote identical balances in 66.6% of pairs on the tuned kinds against 89.2% on general steps, the reverse of the worry that tuning made Haiku's wrong answers more alike. The checks bound the tuning bias; they do not remove it.
claims.tier: disclosure (pre-registered limitations sentence); exploratory (fairness check); pre-specified flag R (reading of the contrast is post hoc)

claims.text: We describe, not explain, why Haiku-medium's votes level off. About a third of pairs of wrong tries on the same puzzle give the identical wrong answer (0.334 pooled; 0.279 chains, 0.404 pieces). Among puzzles with at least 2 wrong tries, 24 of 74 (chains) and 26 of 75 (pieces) had an expected vote score of exactly 0 at the equal-money vote size. On pieces, puzzles with more repetition gained less from voting (Spearman -0.30, 95% interval -0.50 to -0.09); on chains the estimate pointed the same way but its interval includes zero (-0.18, -0.40 to +0.04) (pre-specified descriptive). On chains, repetition is also entangled with mid-range difficulty (post hoc: Spearman 0.50 with accuracy x (100 - accuracy); pieces -0.04), and across the two shapes the pattern runs the other way (post hoc). These describe the level-off; they do not show its cause.
claims.tier: pre-specified descriptive (repeat share, keep-list C9); post hoc (difficulty entanglement, cross-shape reversal)

claims.text: Compounding (a whole answer being right with the per-step rate raised to the number of steps) is a description here, neither shown nor ruled out. In the length sweep (pre-registered descriptive), the reference line uses q = 0.905 (95% interval 0.893 to 0.918), Haiku-medium's share of single pieces right on the pieces shape, pooled over the five lengths; it is a reference, not fitted to the chains. Pieces tracked q^N (observed over predicted 0.91 to 1.12). Chains fell below it at 4 of 5 lengths (0.63, 0.84, 1.20, 0.78 and 0.71 at 4, 6, 8, 12 and 16 steps); the plan says such a shortfall would fit an 'errors breed errors' account but is not tested. A post hoc alternative: chains' own per-step accuracy (each step judged from the model's own previous written balances) was lower, 0.80 to 0.92, and its N-th power comes close to the observed chain scores (0.40 predicted against 0.42 observed at 4 steps; 0.148 against 0.145 at 16). Because that rate is measured after the model's own earlier steps, it is also compatible with errors breeding errors, so the two readings are not separated. The 24-step extrapolation (about 9%) cannot be compared with Pilot 1's near-zero score, which used a different rule mix and presets. For Haiku-max, the drop from 6 to 16 steps (different puzzle sets) is consistent with compounding within the 6-step interval (post hoc).
claims.tier: pre-registered descriptive (length curve); post hoc readings

Each Sonnet and Opus effort point rests on one try per puzzle over 40 bases x 2 shapes (80 answers; exact 95% intervals about 4.5 to 18.6 points wide), except Opus-medium (2 tries per puzzle, 160 answers). In Study 1, Opus-low scored 97.5% against Opus-medium's 96.25% on chains (+1.25 points, 95% interval -3.75 to +7.5; no verdict), both scored 100% on pieces, and Opus-low cost about 7-9% less (exploratory). Opus is near its ceiling here, so the data cannot separate 'effort does not help Opus' from 'these puzzles are too easy for Opus', and effort levels are not ordered where their intervals overlap (for example Opus-high 96.25% against Opus-medium 99.375%).

claims.text: Apart from the plain votes, no multi-call design was money-matched. List cost per puzzle as a share of Opus-medium's was 8.8% for step voting on chains (Test 4), 7.3% for step voting on pieces, 15.5% and 13.5% for the Haiku team, and 25.7% and 21.1% for the picker counting its 8 samples. Test 4 is therefore a cheap decomposition baseline, not an equal-money result. At Opus-medium's price per chain puzzle, step voting could have bought about 25 draws per step, but its locked rule stopped once one answer led by 2 (cap 9; 2.26 draws per step on average), so a budget-matched version was not run and cannot be rebuilt offline. Neither design chose its own split: the puzzle lists its steps, which is why the script split costs nothing, and the team's planner was told to write one instruction per listed step. Scoring step voting from correct inputs gives it no oracle advantage on whole answers: the product of its per-step accuracies is the chance that a chain of independent step calls gets every step right. The results say nothing about decomposing a task whose steps are not given, or about decomposition at Opus-medium's budget.

claims.text: Before the main run, the power model fixed in the plan, fed with the length sweep's measured inputs, forecast that Test 2 would read 'worse by more than the margin' with probability 1.00 at 80 base puzzles ('the pinned power model's forecast under the measured inputs, not a result'). Test 2's reading was therefore expected; what the main run adds is the measured size of the gap (our reading). The forecast covers Test 2 only.

'Effort first, then voting' is a reading across the two studies, not a test. Its within-study anchor: in Study 1, on the same puzzles at nearly the same cost per puzzle, one Haiku-max try scored 97.5% on chains against 49.36% for a 4-try Haiku-medium vote (post hoc reading; Haiku-max is an exploratory arm; no paired interval).

B2 shows that the 6-try Haiku-max vote was no worse than Opus-medium by more than 5 points at about Opus-medium's price: 0.894 of its list cost per answer pooled over shapes (1.091 on chains, 0.733 on pieces). It does not show a saving, and it does not show the vote was better: B2's 95% interval for the difference (-1.15 to +2.44) includes zero, although the 5- and 6-try votes scored higher on point estimate (98.30% and 98.44% against 97.81%). B2's accuracy is the expected accuracy of a 6-try vote estimated from 10 tries per item, not separately run votes. Smaller votes are descriptive only.

claims.text: For a single Haiku-max try, B1 (16 steps): we could not show that a single Haiku-max try is within 5 points of Opus-medium (d -5.19 points, 95% interval -7.75 to -2.69); its error rate was 3.4 times Opus's (95% interval 1.8 to 10.1). B3 (6 steps): we could not show that a single Haiku-max try is within 5 points of Opus-medium (d -3.63, 95% interval -7.0 to -1.5); its error rate was 6.8 times Opus's (95% interval 1.7 to unbounded; Opus-medium made 1 error in 160 tries). A single try cost about 1/6 of Opus-medium's cost per answer at 16 steps and about 1/10 at 6 steps (k measured; list price; descriptive cost beside the tests).

claims.text: Practical advice never puts Opus-medium on a 'drop' list: on fresh puzzles it scored above a single Haiku-max try on point estimate in B1 (97.81% against 92.63%) and B3 (99.38% against 95.75%).

The project's second question, whether cheap models can be trusted as judges, stays largely open: the planned judge study was left out of the project. The only direct data is one exploratory picker: Haiku-medium choosing among 8 of Haiku-medium's own main-run answers, shown in a fixed order. It scored 62.5% (chains) and 67.5% (pieces), and was not shown to beat a plain vote over the same 8 answers (+9.6 points, 95% interval -1.9 to +21.4; +2.1, -6.9 to +10.8; across run windows, same-model flag not fired). Even a perfect picker over those 8 answers would score 87.5% and 86.25%, below Opus-medium's 96.25% and 100%. A second, indirect case is the team's Haiku aggregator, which turned 15 right helper chains wrong and 7 wrong ones right on chains, and 9 and 18 on pieces (counts only). Nothing here tests grading a single answer, a stronger judge or judging max-effort answers; the paper does not generalise to LLM-as-judge.

user_framing_choices.question: Does Test 3 appear in the abstract?
user_framing_choices.background: Test 3 compared the equal-money Haiku-medium vote with one Sonnet-medium answer on chains. Under the official marking rule it reads 'worse by more than 10 points', but under the original rule (before Deviation 2, which was adopted after seeing Sonnet's replies) and when copy slips are forgiven it reads inconclusive. Its pieces counterpart is also inconclusive.
user_framing_choices.why_it_matters: Abstract sentences get quoted without their qualifiers. Test 3 is the one Study 1 reading that changes with the marking rule.
user_framing_choices.option_a: Keep Test 3 out of the abstract; report it in Results with its marking-rule qualifier (sweep A).
user_framing_choices.option_b: Include Test 3 in the abstract with a short qualifier.
user_framing_choices.option_merged: The abstract names Tests 1-2 and 4 (which read the same under both marking rules) and Test 5; Test 3 appears in Results with its one-line qualifier, and the four-view table goes in the appendix.
user_framing_choices.why: Keeps the abstract to readings that hold under both rules, and still reports Test 3 fully where its qualifier can travel with it, as D-90 asked ('should not overcomplicate the reader').

user_framing_choices.question: Should the paper include a practitioner frontier or a cost-for-target-accuracy table?
user_framing_choices.background: The pre-registered fitted frontier (C6) was dropped by ruling. The blind review wants a buying guide that shows the cheapest route to a target accuracy. The sweep says any such table must be a post hoc reading of measured points, with nothing fitted.
user_framing_choices.why_it_matters: Practitioners will read such a table as advice. Its points come from different studies, puzzle sets and dates, so mislabelling would overstate the evidence.
user_framing_choices.option_a: No frontier; describe measured points in the text only (sweep A's caution).
user_framing_choices.option_b: Add a buying guide and a cost-for-target table (blind review B).
user_framing_choices.option_merged: One post hoc table of measured points (accuracy and list cost per answer), each labelled by study, puzzle set, date and tier, with cross-set points marked descriptive; no fitted curve; in the appendix with a two-sentence pointer in the Discussion.
user_framing_choices.why: It gives readers what they need to re-price, stays inside the 'no fitted frontier' ruling, and keeps the main text uncluttered.

user_framing_choices.question: How candidly does the paper say that the confirmatory tests did not test the lever that mattered (the cheap model's effort)?
user_framing_choices.background: Study 1's five tests kept Haiku at medium effort; Haiku-max was an exploratory extra, first in the cut order, and became a test only in Study 1b. The blind review frames this as a lesson about design priors; the sweep treats it as the surprise.
user_framing_choices.why_it_matters: It shapes how the story of the Haiku-max surprise reads: luck, or a lesson others can use when designing such studies.
user_framing_choices.option_a: Tell it only as the surprise (sweep A).
user_framing_choices.option_b: Present it as a lesson about design priors (blind review B).
user_framing_choices.option_merged: Keep the Haiku-max surprise as the story's turn (D-125), and add one candid Discussion paragraph naming the design-prior lesson, labelled as our reading; not in the abstract or title.
user_framing_choices.why: D-121 delegated the journey and the story's telling to the team, and D-125 fixed the surprise as the turn; one Discussion paragraph adds the useful lesson without competing with the headline.

reviewer_risks.risk: One synthetic task family, with rule kinds developed on Haiku's own slips.
reviewer_risks.answer: Scope the title, abstract and every claim to exact-answer, multi-step rule-following puzzles of this family; present a careful case study plus a reusable equal-money, pre-registered protocol; give the two-sided bias table and its checks; name the dropped code family and the unrun ArXivMath check as future work (L-36, L-52).

reviewer_risks.risk: One vendor's models, studied with that vendor's AI tools and paid with its credit.
reviewer_risks.answer: Scoring is mechanical exact matching by locked code with no LLM judge; locks 1-4 carry public timestamps; analyses re-ran byte-identically; costs agreed with the Console within one cent. The AI-use statement follows D-129 (tools under the authors' direction; Anthropic had no role; models, tools and credit disclosed as Anthropic's); separation between AI sessions is never called 'independent' (L-38).

reviewer_risks.risk: Study 1's Sonnet comparator ran one level below its default effort, which colours Tests 3 and 5.
reviewer_risks.answer: Say so beside Tests 3 and 5 and every Opus-versus-Sonnet cost comparison; note Opus-low was also below its default; Test 5 supports only the accuracy half of 'bigger model, less thinking'; show Study 1b's Sonnet-high point as a labelled post hoc, cross-study reading (L-19).

reviewer_risks.risk: Near-ceiling comparator and lenient margins: B1 and B3 pass the 10-point secondary margin with 3.4 and 6.8 times Opus-medium's errors; B2's 5-point margin was chosen after Study 1's exploratory result.
reviewer_risks.answer: Give the error-rate ratio beside every d; put the exact bound beside intervals that collapse at 100%; state why the margins are 10 and 5; show B1's errors are wrong states, not format; report the pre-registered near-ceiling label; say the design cannot show where Opus-medium pulls ahead (L-35, G1-10, G2-20).

reviewer_risks.risk: Novelty: majority voting, voting plateaus and multi-agent results at matched tokens are known.
reviewer_risks.answer: Add Related Work; use the term cost-of-pass; say which known effects our data echo; state that the team and step-voting arms were not money- or token-matched so they do not test the multi-agent result; claim novelty narrowly (equal dollars on one ladder, effort as an axis, exact scoring, public locks, disclosed deviations) (L-39).

reviewer_risks.risk: Winner's curse: the Haiku-max idea came from an exploratory arm, and Study 1b's margin, cap and length were chosen after Study 1's results were opened.
reviewer_risks.answer: Study 1b tested it on 400 never-sent puzzles frozen before any Haiku-max data, under a publicly timestamped lock, with k from cost-only rows; write 'tested again on fresh puzzles from the same generator and preset family', never 'replicated' (L-12).

reviewer_risks.risk: No latency data for the recommended setting (Haiku-max); the 5-try vote time is computed, not measured.
reviewer_risks.answer: State the limit plainly; give medium-effort medians and the computed vote times as computed; offer the thinking-token proxy labelled as our reading; no latency claim for Haiku-max (L-44, X-39).

reviewer_risks.risk: Tests 1-4's 'worse' readings come from unadjusted intervals because Holm stopped at Test 3.
reviewer_risks.answer: The three-way reading was pre-registered; Tests 1, 2 and 4's upper ends lie 13.75 to 20 points beyond the margin, Test 3's 2.2 points; report a Holm-adjusted inferiority check or 99% intervals from the locked bootstrap code as a post hoc sensitivity; Test 3 is the reading that could change (L-08).

reviewer_risks.risk: The marking rule was changed after seeing Sonnet's replies, and the change helped Sonnet.
reviewer_risks.answer: Deviation 2 was declared before any main-run data, applies to every model, and both rules are reported; it narrowed Test 5's gap (Test 5 holds under both) and is why Test 3 reads 'worse'; Tests 1, 2 and 4 are unchanged; full original-rule tables in the appendix (L-16, L-14, G1-11).

reviewer_risks.risk: The move from 24 to 6 steps (Deviation 1) could have created the negative vote result or picked a length that favours one side.
reviewer_risks.answer: At 24 steps Haiku-medium scored near zero against Opus-medium's 96% and 88%, so the negative result did not depend on the move; the move was ruled blind to Pilot 1's Opus and Sonnet results and N was picked by a Haiku-only rule with the length sweep's Opus and Sonnet answers sealed (G2-12, L-18).

reviewer_risks.risk: Tuning bias: rule kinds tuned against Haiku.
reviewer_risks.answer: Report the spec's two-sided bias table ('the net direction is not known in advance'), the fairness check (targeting index 0.82, 0.43 to 1.37; Opus side nearly empty) and flag R (less agreement on the tuned kinds); the checks bound the bias, they do not remove it (L-52, L-53, L-54).

reviewer_risks.risk: The main lesson ('effort first, then voting') rests on a cross-study reading.
reviewer_risks.answer: Label it our reading; anchor it within Study 1 (one Haiku-max try 97.5% against a 4-try Haiku-medium vote's 49.36% at nearly the same cost on chains; post hoc, exploratory arm); add free within-study Study 1b comparisons labelled post hoc (L-49).

reviewer_risks.risk: Equal-money tests answer a different question from a buyer's 'cheapest route to a target accuracy', and k does not transfer.
reviewer_risks.answer: Say so in Methods; show how k depends on price ratio, effort, shape and length; give the cost ratio per length; offer a labelled post hoc re-pricing table and, if the user agrees, a cost-for-target table (L-41, L-42, L-43).

reviewer_risks.risk: Small samples and wide intervals (one try over 40 bases for most effort points; 20-base same-model check; 10-puzzle real-time check).
reviewer_risks.answer: Give interval widths; power was simulated and locked before each study's data; say what each check could and could not detect; never order overlapping effort points (G1-20, L-61).

reviewer_risks.risk: Puzzle sets differ in difficulty and no drift check links Study 1 and Study 1b.
reviewer_risks.answer: Keep every cross-study and cross-set comparison descriptive; take length comparisons from one study's sets; state that the same-model check covers the top-up window only and cannot rule out 8-10-point shifts (L-48, G1-19, L-47).

reviewer_risks.risk: Effort labels are not a common unit across models; effort, tokens and token limits are confounded.
reviewer_risks.answer: Define effort as the API's value; compare models by dollars and, descriptively, by measured tokens (shared tokenizer); never 'accuracy follows tokens, not the label' (L-93, L-32).

reviewer_risks.risk: Analysis code and reporting definitions were written after lock 3.
reviewer_risks.answer: The driver was publicly stamped after collection and before any result was opened; the definitions were approved before results; all post-lock code and definitions are listed in the appendix; tier labels say where each item was fixed (L-69, L-71, L-72, L-64).

reviewer_risks.risk: Reproducibility: raw records not yet released; some run commits and a re-run exist only on unmerged branches.
reviewer_risks.answer: Release calls.jsonl and compact tables with hashes matching the public stamps; add a commit table and tool versions; merge and tag (needs the user's yes); venue and licence are the user's rulings (L-84, L-85, G2-25).

reviewer_risks.risk: Step voting is scored from correct inputs (an apparent oracle) and was far cheaper than Opus-medium.
reviewer_risks.answer: Correct-input scoring equals the chance that a chain of independent step calls gets every step right, so it gives no oracle advantage on whole answers; Test 4 is presented as a cheap decomposition baseline, not an equal-money result, and a budget-matched version could not be rebuilt offline (G2-11, L-21, G2-19).

reviewer_risks.risk: The locked texts and stamped result files use the word 'matches'.
reviewer_risks.answer: Say once in Method that the pre-registration's 'matches' meant non-inferiority within the margin and is written 'no worse than X by more than N points'; map stamped labels in the data README; quote locked text only as marked quotations (G1-16, L-03, G3-05).

reviewer_risks.risk: Prompt-wording sensitivity of Haiku-medium.
reviewer_risks.answer: Report the +8.75-point shift with its interval (0.0 to +17.25), its small format share, and its scale against Tests 1-4's gaps; not checked at max effort (L-57, G1-15).

reviewer_risks.risk: Batch versus real time.
reviewer_risks.answer: Say 'measured in Batch'; the real-time subsets are tiny and point in mixed directions, so no Batch effect is claimed either way (L-45, G1-13).

reviewer_risks.risk: Test 2's result was forecast before the run, so it may look uninformative.
reviewer_risks.answer: Disclose the forecast (Test 2 only); the run adds the measured size of the gap (our reading) (L-51).

reviewer_risks.risk: Test puzzles partly shown in helper sessions.
reviewer_risks.answer: Never shown to a model under test; the pre-registered sensitivity without them gives the same B1-B3 readings; descriptive outputs not re-run; no scan recorded for Study 1's set (L-75, G2-16).

claims.section: What drives it (descriptive): the length curve
claims.text: Pre-specified descriptive (D-87 length curve), already computed. The reference line uses q = 0.9053 (95% interval 0.8925 to 0.9180), Haiku-medium's per-piece accuracy on pieces pooled over the five lengths; nothing is tuned to chains. Observed whole-answer accuracy over q^N: chains 0.625, 0.835, 1.197, 0.775 and 0.712 at 4, 6, 8, 12 and 16 steps; pieces 1.027, 0.908, 1.119, 1.006 and 1.056. On point estimates, chains fall below the independent-pieces line at 4 of 5 lengths (not at 8); pieces stay near it. The plan's own caveat applies: a chain ratio below 1 would fit the 'errors breed errors' account, but it is not tested. A post hoc alternative reading: against chains' own per-step rate (each step judged from the model's own previous balances: 0.796, 0.865, 0.916, 0.864, 0.888), the predicted chain scores are 0.40, 0.42, 0.50, 0.17 and 0.15 against observed 0.42, 0.46, 0.54, 0.235 and 0.145, so the shortfall appears as a lower per-step rate on chains, which earlier slips may themselves cause; these data do not separate the two readings. 20 bases per length; point ratios only.
