user_framing_choices.question: Should any paid run happen before the API credit expires on 2026-10-19 UTC?
user_framing_choices.background: All paid runs are done and checked. Your ruling D-116 keeps the remaining credit (spend log: $95.84) unused unless the reviews find a crucial gap that only a small paid run can close. Both reviews, and this compile of the analyses rows and the gap rows, found none.
user_framing_choices.why_it_matters: A paid run now would need a written plan, a public lock, a trial round, Edith's check and your go within four days, and no option on the table can change any test result.
user_framing_choices.option_a: Review A: no crucial gap. If you still want one, the max-effort latency check is the one most likely to count (A priced it at $2-4; by our arithmetic it is about $7.84 at list).
user_framing_choices.option_b: Review B: implies gaps (a 24-step test; Opus-low against Sonnet at its default effort) and frames them as tests without the lock cost. A new 24-step test cannot be locked in time, and the Sonnet comparison can be done free on data we already have (X-04).
user_framing_choices.option_merged: No paid run. The paper states three limits plainly (no max-effort latency; the Haiku-max vote tested only at 16 steps; in Study 1b, Sonnet and Opus-low only at 6 steps), and the days go to the free analyses.
user_framing_choices.recommendation: The merged option: no paid run.
user_framing_choices.why: Nothing a paid run could buy changes a headline, the free analyses answer most of what the reviews raised, and four days leaves no safe room for a lock and a run.

user_framing_choices.question: Does the practical 'what should I buy' view (cost against accuracy at each length, plus a table of the cheapest setting that reaches 90%, 95% and 98%) lead the results, or support them?
user_framing_choices.background: The pre-registered fitted frontier was dropped before the data (D-94(5)). Both reviews still want a practical view. It can be built free from numbers we already have, labelled post hoc, with nothing fitted.
user_framing_choices.why_it_matters: It is the most direct answer to the paper's budget question, but it is post hoc. Leading with it would put an untested view in front of the tests.
user_framing_choices.option_a: A: one post hoc frontier per length, every point labelled by study, puzzle set and tier, never presented as the dropped pre-registered item.
user_framing_choices.option_b: B: adds the cost-for-target-accuracy table, which answers a buyer's question directly.
user_framing_choices.option_merged: Both: one figure and one table in the effort-and-length section, pointed to from the Discussion. The lead stays the story you confirmed (the Haiku-max surprise, D-125).
user_framing_choices.recommendation: The merged option: the view supports the story and does not lead it.
user_framing_choices.why: The tests and the surprise stay first, and readers still get the practical answer.

user_framing_choices.question: For readers who need exact answers, should we stress the error-rate ratio (how many times more often a setting was wrong than Opus-medium), or keep it as a companion beside the accuracy difference?
user_framing_choices.background: The tests compare accuracy differences in points. Near 100% a small point gap can hide a large error ratio: by point estimate a single Haiku-max try made 3.37 times (B1) and 6.8 times (B3) Opus-medium's errors, with wide intervals (1.78 to 10.07; 1.67 to unbounded).
user_framing_choices.why_it_matters: It changes emphasis, not any result, but it shapes what readers take away about single Haiku-max tries.
user_framing_choices.option_a: A: the ratio beside every Study 1b test, as the Study 1b plan requires.
user_framing_choices.option_b: B: also beside Tests 1-2, with B1's and B3's intervals printed, but worded 'reliably a few points worse', which is not allowed for an inconclusive test.
user_framing_choices.option_merged: The ratio beside all eight tests, with B1's and B3's intervals printed as labelled description. The accuracy difference stays the headline number, and the ratio is stressed once in the Discussion for exactness-critical uses.
user_framing_choices.why: The tests were designed on points; the ratio is the honest companion near the ceiling.

user_framing_choices.question: Does Study 1's 3-try Haiku-max vote appear as one line beside Tests 1-2 in the main text?
user_framing_choices.background: In Study 1 the 3 Haiku-max tries drawn per puzzle, voted, scored 100.0 and 98.75 against Opus-medium's 96.25 and 100.0. That is exploratory, and not an equal-money vote: it cost about a third and a quarter of Opus-medium's price. This result is why Study 1b exists.
user_framing_choices.why_it_matters: It is the turn that explains the method: the surprise that led to a second, locked study. You delegated how much of the journey goes in the main text (D-121(4)).
user_framing_choices.option_a: A: keep it in the Haiku-max surprise section only.
user_framing_choices.option_b: B: place it beside Tests 1-2, but B calls it 'equal-money', which the file contradicts (k was capped at the 3 tries drawn).
user_framing_choices.option_merged: One labelled exploratory line beside Tests 1-2 saying the vote was capped at 3 tries and cost about 0.33 and 0.25 of Opus-medium's price, then the Study 1b section tests it properly.
user_framing_choices.recommendation: The team's decision: the merged option.
user_framing_choices.why: It explains in one line why Study 1b was run, without overstating an exploratory result.

user_framing_choices.question: Should the cost table also give cost per 10,000 puzzles in plain dollars?
user_framing_choices.background: At list price on Study 1's 6-step chains, 10,000 puzzles would cost about $402 with Opus-medium, $147 with Sonnet-medium, $44 with one Haiku-max try and $11 with one Haiku-medium try (half that at Batch prices).
user_framing_choices.why_it_matters: It makes the cost gaps concrete for a general reader. Without the accuracies beside them, the dollars could mislead.
user_framing_choices.option_a: A: not proposed.
user_framing_choices.option_b: B: proposes it as reader framing.
user_framing_choices.option_merged: Use it once, in the cost discussion, always with each setting's accuracy beside it (96.25, 80.0, 97.5 and 43.72) and Haiku-max labelled exploratory.
user_framing_choices.why: It fits the plain-words voice you chose and is post hoc arithmetic on locked costs.

must_not_claim: Any saving or 'k tries are enough' claim from a post hoc k at 16 steps presented as confirmatory: Study 1b pre-registered 'B2's k-sensitivity: none'. Report every k, not only the smallest whose lower end clears -5.
'Haiku-max's errors rarely repeat', or any mechanism for B2, before X-08 is computed. Even after it is computed, describe only; make no causal claim.
That the Haiku-max gap to Opus-medium widens with length. The 6- and 16-step intervals overlap and each length used a different puzzle set (G2-23).
That a bigger model at low effort beats a smaller one at its default effort, whether from Test 5 or from X-04.
'Equal-money' for Study 1's 3-try Haiku-max vote: k was capped at the 3 tries drawn, and the equal-money k is 9 on chains and 11 on pieces.
That Haiku's accuracy rose with effort 'in every shape'. It holds on pooled points only (6-step chains: Haiku-low 52.5, Haiku-medium 52.0).
'Sonnet and Opus-low were run only at 6 steps' without 'in Study 1b'. The length sweep has Sonnet-medium at 12 and 16 steps.
That the 5-try vote latency was measured (it was computed from single calls), or any latency result for Haiku-max.
'Chains compound faster than independent steps' as a finding. The plan says a ratio below 1 'would fit' errors-breed-errors, and it is not tested.
That thinking-off's near-zero at 16 steps is mostly a format failure: 0 of the 112 well-formed chain replies were right.
'Opus-high's 96.25 is one miss' (it is 3 misses in 80), 'Opus-high is worse', or 'the Opus dip'. Write 'Opus 96.25-100, not rising steadily with effort'.
'Picking helps on chains, re-working helps on pieces'. Picker minus vote@8 on chains is +9.64 (-1.875 to +21.35).
That E3 given Opus-medium's budget would get about 13 draws per step (the stamped costs give about 25). Never use the barred word 'matched' in any compound (budget-, token-).
Any multiplicity-corrected reading of Tests 1-4 before it is computed with a correction fixed in advance.
B1's or B3's interval as a test result ('reliably a few points worse').
The cascade as 'the most promising route', or any pre-judged result for a free analysis not yet run.
That on chains, wrong-answer repetition is 'only weakly related to difficulty' (Spearman 0.50 with mid-range difficulty; G2-02).
That the post hoc frontier replaces the dropped fitted frontier (C6), or any fitted frontier.
The Haiku picker's gain over vote@8 as shown: both intervals include 0.
disclosures: Every post hoc analysis is a separate labelled script, run after all locked results were opened. It reads only the stamped raw files, checks them against the public data stamps (D-93, D-109, D-113) and writes its own result file. Each number enters the claims ledger, with source, key and tier, before any text uses it (X-37). Today the raw compact tables of all three runs agree with their stamped hashes.
Study 1b pre-registered no k-sensitivity for B2 ('none', spec §4). The vote curves at 6 and 12 steps and every k other than 6 are post hoc descriptive.
The pre-registered fitted frontier and time axis (C6) were dropped before the data (D-94(5)). Any frontier shown is post hoc, and nothing is fitted.

Item 9e's cascade definitions were pre-specified for Haiku-medium; applying them to Haiku-max is post hoc. Item 20's difficulty bins were defined on Haiku-medium accuracy; any 16-step use says which accuracy sets the bins.
Real-time latency was measured only at medium effort, on 10 puzzles from one machine on one day. The 5-try vote time is computed from single calls.
In Study 1b, Sonnet and Opus-low ran only at 6 steps (the length sweep has Sonnet-medium at 12 and 16 steps, 20 bases, one try, other sets).
The appendix lists every descriptive, exploratory and post hoc estimate with its tier, plus the total count; an optional Benjamini-Hochberg column is labelled post hoc (X-35).
The original-rule format figures come from secondary.rates.format_compliance_original. The original_repeat_rule_appendix.format_compliance block repeats the official values (G2-28).

reviewer_risks.risk: Forking paths: many post hoc analyses added after the results were opened.
reviewer_risks.answer: Every one is labelled post hoc or exploratory, gets no verdict and runs as its own hash-checked script with its own result file (X-37). The appendix lists every estimate with its tier and the total count (X-35). Where a choice of k is involved, all k are reported (X-02).

reviewer_risks.risk: The 'effort first, then voting' message rests on a reading across studies with different puzzles.
reviewer_risks.answer: X-03 checks 'effort first' on the same puzzles at equal money, in Study 1 and in Study 1b, and X-01 adds the Haiku-max vote at 6 and 12 steps. Until then the message carries 'our reading, not a test'.

reviewer_risks.risk: Tests 1-4's 'worse by more than the margin' readings use unadjusted intervals.
reviewer_risks.answer: X-12 recomputes them with a correction fixed in advance. Only Test 3 is near the margin (upper end -12.20), and it already reads inconclusive under two scoring views, which the paper shows (X-17).

reviewer_risks.risk: Bootstrap intervals collapse to [100, 100] at Opus's ceiling and suggest false certainty.
reviewer_risks.answer: X-13 replaces every degenerate interval with an exact one on the error count, as the approved style sheet requires. Error-rate ratios sit beside every difference (X-14).

reviewer_risks.risk: Test 5 set Opus-low against Sonnet one level below Sonnet's default effort.
reviewer_risks.answer: X-04 gives free paired comparisons of Sonnet-high on Study 1b's 40 six-step bases, labelled cross-study against Test 5. Test 5's text says Sonnet ran one level below its default.

reviewer_risks.risk: The Haiku picker chose reply 1 in 81 of 160 puzzles, which suggests position bias.
reviewer_risks.answer: X-19 adds a 'take reply 1' baseline, accuracy by picked position and agreement with the plurality answer. Position effects were not studied, and the paper says so.

reviewer_risks.risk: The small vote's cost companion: at k = 6 the pooled B2 vote cost about 1.09 of Opus-medium's price on chains.
reviewer_risks.answer: B2 always travels with its per-shape costs (style sheet), and X-02 gives each shape's own equal-money k (5 on chains, 8 on pieces) with paired intervals.

reviewer_risks.risk: Small samples: Study 1b's effort points rest on 40 bases with one try each; the same-model check on 20 bases.
reviewer_risks.answer: Intervals everywhere, exact where needed, no ordering of overlapping effort points, and a statement beside each check of what it could detect (G1-20).

reviewer_risks.risk: Thinking-off's 0.5% floor is read as pure reasoning failure, or as a format artefact.
reviewer_risks.answer: X-18 splits format failures from wrong answers. None of the 112 well-formed 16-step chain replies was right.

reviewer_risks.risk: No max-effort latency.
reviewer_risks.answer: State the limit, give medium-effort latencies, give output tokens as a labelled proxy and say the vote time is computed. Under D-116 a paid check is not crucial.

Under the 1/m tie rule a 2-try vote is expected to score about the single-try rate, so the xhigh rows are expected near 58.375 (16 steps) and 76.75 (6 steps). Report what the data give.

free_analyses.analysis: 6. X-12, multiplicity-corrected readings of Tests 1-4. Recompute the 'worse by more than the margin' readings with a correction fixed in advance, using the locked paired BCa code and seeds: either Holm across the four (H0 d >= -10) or 99% intervals from the same draws. State which still exclude -10. Current unadjusted upper ends: Test 3 -12.20 (closest to the margin); Tests 1, 2 and 4 at -23.75, -26.96 and -30.0. The two corrections can differ for Test 3: Holm's step-down judges the largest p at the unadjusted level once the other three clear theirs, while a 99% interval is uniformly stricter. So the correction is fixed before computing (Edith queue), and the outcome is stated only after.
free_analyses.why: Holm adjusted only the 'no worse than' claim, which only Test 5 made. The template readings of Tests 1-4 use unadjusted intervals, which a reviewer will flag.

parts.paid_run_verdict:
No paid run. Nothing in the 44 analyses rows or the gap rows shows a crucial gap that only paid data could close (D-116).

Every headline (Tests 1-5, B1-B3) rests on completed, locked runs, and no paid option could change any of them. The gaps the reviews name are limits the paper states:
1. Latency was measured only at medium effort, on 10 puzzles; the 5-try vote time is computed, not measured.
2. The Haiku-max vote was tested only at 16 steps, and no length run shows where Opus-medium pulls ahead of it. The free X-01 adds descriptive vote curves at 6 and 12 steps.
3. In Study 1b, Sonnet and Opus-low ran only at 6 steps. The length sweep has Sonnet-medium at 12 and 16 steps.

If the user still wants a paid run, the options are:
- A max-effort latency check: about $7.84 at list by our arithmetic. A priced it at $2-4. Real-time calls get no Batch discount, and D-94(5) dropped the time axis, so it also needs a ruling.
- A descriptive 24-step Haiku-max vs Opus-medium run: about $8-12 at Batch (A's estimate, unchecked).
- Sonnet-high and Opus-low at 16 steps: about $8-16 at Batch, cap about $25 (A's estimate, unchecked).

Each would need a spec, a lock, a trial round, Edith's clearance, a spend-log row and the user's go before the credit expires on 2026-10-19 UTC, four days from now. Each would also add a comparison across run windows that no drift check links. The value is small: each turns one stated limit into one descriptive point.

Dropped:
- A new confirmatory Opus-low vs Sonnet-high test (X-42): X-04 covers it free on existing data.
- A Haiku-max wording check (X-43, about $1): low value.

Remaining credit by the spend log: $95.83793820 (the Console read $95.87 after the top-up).

Recommendation: no paid run. State the three limits, and spend the remaining days on the free analyses, from the top of the ranked list.

claims.text: The abstract and introduction open with the budget question and the effort-first answer, labelled as a post hoc synthesis, plus its two confirmatory anchors: Tests 1-2 (6-step puzzles, Study 1's main run: at no more than Opus-medium's price, a Haiku-medium vote was worse than one Opus-medium answer by more than 10 points) and B2 (fresh 16-step puzzles, Study 1b: a 6-try Haiku-max vote was no worse than one Opus-medium answer by more than 5 points, at 0.894 of its price per answer, pooled). The two anchors come from different studies, sets and lengths, so any comparison between them is descriptive. The body keeps D-116's three parts in study order.

Study 1's confirmatory tests answered a narrower question than the brief. Tests 1-4 held the cheap model at medium effort (its API default; medium is also Opus's default) and varied only votes and step splitting. Test 5 compared Opus-low with Sonnet-medium (a bigger model at less thinking). Raising the cheap model's effort above its default was not among the tests: Haiku-max x3 was an exploratory extra, listed first to trim in the budget plan (D-27). Its Study 1 result, the Haiku-max surprise (exploratory), led to Study 1b, a separate pre-registration on fresh, never-sent puzzles (lock 4). Its Tests B1-B3 are confirmatory comparisons of Haiku-max with Opus-medium. The effort contrast itself (Haiku-medium against Haiku-max) is pre-specified descriptive (the effort sweep), not a test. We state the omission plainly, as a lesson about which levers the design expected to matter, not only as a surprise.

claims.text: Pre-specified descriptive, with no causal claim. claims.section: Top-up results and Limits ('What we did not answer')
claims.text: Whether a cheap model can be trusted as a judge was not studied: the planned grading study (Study 5) was left out of this project early, before Study 1 ran (D-44). Even a perfect picker over these 8 medium-effort answers stays below Opus-medium's 96.25 and 100 (descriptive, no paired interval). A second, indirect case is the Haiku team's aggregator (exploratory; counts only): on chains it turned 15 right helper answers wrong and 7 wrong ones right; on pieces 9 right answers wrong and 18 wrong ones right. The judge question stays open; a judge study, including judging max-effort answers, is future work. No generalisation to LLM-as-judge grading.

user_framing_choices.question: The one sentence a reader should remember
user_framing_choices.background: You asked the team to choose this from the results (D-121, item 6). The working candidate is 'effort first, then voting' from D-116, which you approved as a candidate. Its first summary used two phrases our wording rules now forbid, so it has to be reworded before it goes in.
user_framing_choices.why_it_matters: It becomes the last line of the abstract and the first line of the conclusion, and it is what a reader repeats. If it says more than the data show (that it was tested, or that it holds for every cheap model), a reviewer will catch it.
user_framing_choices.option_a: (Opus) 'Effort first, then voting': raising Haiku 5.5's thinking effort to max helped far more than any multi-call design tried at medium effort. Labelled as our reading across both studies, for one synthetic puzzle family, Claude 5.5 models, short prompts and list prices of 2026-10-12/13.
user_framing_choices.option_b: (Fable) 'Buy thinking before you buy votes': thinking first, then a small odd-sized vote of the thinking-heavy setting; buy the bigger model only for the last few points, at 2-10 times the cost per correct answer; do not buy default-effort samples, teams or cheap judges.
user_framing_choices.option_merged: Effort first, then voting: for the cheap model studied here (Haiku 5.5) on exact multi-step puzzles, raise its thinking effort before you buy more of its tries; the next step is a small vote of max-effort tries. (Our reading across both studies, not a test; one synthetic ledger family at 6-16 steps, Claude 5.5 models only, short prompts, list prices of 2026-10-12/13.)
user_framing_choices.recommendation: Team decision: the merged sentence. It closes the abstract and opens the conclusion, always with its 'our reading, not a test' label and the scope.
user_framing_choices.why: It keeps the label you approved in D-116 and adds Fable's plain 'raise it before you buy more'. It drops three Fable extras the files do not support: 'odd-sized' (the one tested vote used 6 tries), '2-10 times' (no single stamped figure) and 'do not buy cheap judges' (we ran one picker; the judge study was dropped, D-44). It names Haiku 5.5 because it is the only cheap model tested. Each half has a basis. Within Study 1, on the same puzzles at about the same cost, one Haiku-max try scored 97.5 / 95.0 against 49.36 / 58.95 for a 4-try Haiku-medium vote (post hoc; Haiku-max was an exploratory arm). In Study 1b, a 6-try Haiku-max vote was no worse than one Opus-medium answer by more than 5 points (B2, confirmatory). Votes also removed a far larger share of errors at max effort (about 79% at 6 tries) than at medium (about 26-32%) (post hoc arithmetic).

user_framing_choices.question: What the paper leads with
user_framing_choices.background: The current outline opens with 'Cheap votes lost'. Both reviews want the lead to move to effort. You ruled the three-part structure (Study 1, Study 1b, the top-up; D-116), and you confirmed that the story turns on the Haiku-max surprise, with two smaller surprises (D-125).
user_framing_choices.why_it_matters: The first paragraph decides what the reader thinks the paper is about. Leading with the negatives alone reads as 'cheap models lose'. Leading with Haiku-max alone invites 'they found one good result after looking'.
user_framing_choices.option_a: (Opus) Lead with the budget question and 'effort first, then voting', and keep the three parts in study order. Two acts: at medium effort, cheap tries did not pay (Tests 1-2 and 4); then turning Haiku's effort up to max changed the picture (Study 1b).
user_framing_choices.option_b: (Fable) Re-centre the whole paper on effort, with voting and teams secondary, and open by admitting that the pre-registered part answered a narrower question than the brief.
user_framing_choices.option_merged: The abstract and introduction open with the budget question and the effort-first answer, labelled as our reading, plus two confirmatory anchors. First, Tests 1-2 (6 steps): at no more than Opus-medium's price, a Haiku-medium vote was worse than one Opus-medium answer by more than 10 points. Second, B2 (fresh 16-step puzzles): a 6-try Haiku-max vote was no worse than one Opus-medium answer by more than 5 points, at 0.894 of its price. Comparing the two anchors is descriptive, since they come from different studies, sets and days, and no drift check links them. Introduction findings in this order: (1) at medium effort, cheap tries fell short (Tests 1-2 and 4, scoped); (2) the Haiku-max surprise and its fresh test (B2; B1 and B3 with error ratios and cost); (3) the two smaller surprises: Haiku-medium's wrong answers often repeat and its votes level off (described, no cause claimed), and the starting guess failed (Haiku-medium wrote about as many output tokens as Opus-medium, so the per-task price gap stayed near the list ratio, 36.6x and 44.0x); (4) Test 5 with its Sonnet caveat; (5) the effort sweep; (6) the top-up's designs (exploratory). The body keeps study order. The token finding stays out of the title and the headline sentence.
user_framing_choices.why: It follows D-116 and D-125 directly. Both anchors are confirmatory, so the opening rests on tests, and the one reading that spans both studies is labelled as such. In the body the reader meets the plan, the clear negative, the surprise and the fresh test in that order, which is the storyline (C) you chose for the voice. The second surprise is worded without 'so', because the data show the repeats and the plateau together but not that one causes the other.

user_framing_choices.question: How the confirmatory negatives are framed (including the 'narrower question' point and Test 3 in the abstract)
user_framing_choices.background: Study 1's five tests were fixed in advance. Tests 1-4 came out 'worse by more than 10 points' and Test 5 'no worse'. The lever that turned out to matter, raising Haiku's thinking effort, was not one of them: Haiku-max was an extra, listed first to cut if money ran short (D-27). Reading blind, Fable says the pre-registered part 'answered a narrower question than the brief' and 'tested the wrong lever'. Opus tells the effort result as a surprise.
user_framing_choices.why_it_matters: Anyone who reads our public budget plan can see this. Saying it ourselves is stronger than being caught. But Fable's version gets two facts wrong. Test 5 used Opus-low, so not every test held effort at medium. And the answer did not come only from an exploratory arm, because B2 is confirmatory. Test 3 also changes its reading under a marking rule, so it is not a clean negative.
user_framing_choices.option_a: (Opus) Tell it as a turn: at medium effort, cheap tries did not pay; turning Haiku's effort up to max changed the picture. The exploratory surprise became Tests B1-B3 through a new lock on fresh puzzles.
user_framing_choices.option_b: (Fable) Say that the confirmatory family tested the wrong lever: five tests held every model at medium effort, four came back as clean negatives that hold under every view, and the answer came from an arm marked first to trim. Tell it as a lesson about the design's assumptions.
user_framing_choices.option_merged: A plain paragraph in the introduction: Study 1's confirmatory tests answered a narrower question than the brief. Tests 1-4 held Haiku at medium effort (its API default, as it is for Opus) and varied only votes and step splitting. Test 5 compared Opus-low with Sonnet-medium. Raising Haiku's effort was not tested in Study 1, because Haiku-max was an exploratory extra, first to trim. It led to Study 1b, a separate pre-registration on fresh puzzles, whose B1-B3 are confirmatory. The effort contrast itself is descriptive. The paragraph is told as a lesson about which levers the design expected to matter, not only as a surprise. Each negative is scoped. Tests 1, 2 and 4 give the same reading in every pre-registered scoring view. Test 3 is fragile: it is inconclusive under the original marking rule (+0.30 [-13.58, +14.95]) and when copy slips are forgiven, and its pieces counterpart (exploratory) also read inconclusive. It is never grouped as a clean negative. Test 4 is a cheap decomposition baseline at 0.088 of Opus-medium's cost, not an equal-money result. Tests 1-2 ran at 'no more than' Opus-medium's price (0.984 and 0.909 of it). Deviation 1 is named where the tests first appear. The main text gives one original-rule line beside Tests 3 and 5, and the full four-view table goes in the appendix.
user_framing_choices.recommendation: The merged option, with Test 3 kept out of the abstract (Results only, with its qualifier).
user_framing_choices.why: It keeps Fable's honest lesson in plain words and uses Opus's knowledge of the rulings (D-27, D-96, D-98) to fix Fable's two errors. 'Wrong lever' is dropped as too loaded. Test 3 stays out of the abstract because its reading turns on a marking rule adopted after Sonnet's length-sweep replies were seen (D-90), so it would need two qualifiers there. The layout follows your D-90 condition that the marking rule 'should not overcomplicate the reader'. It also settles a contradiction between two compiled rows (X-17 against L-17) in favour of L-17's split.

user_framing_choices.question: How Test 5 is framed beside the Sonnet-high result
user_framing_choices.background: Test 5 is Study 1's only result declared under the correction for running several tests: Opus-low was no worse than Sonnet-medium by more than 10 points. But Sonnet's default effort is high, so Study 1 ran it one level below. Study 1b's effort sweep later ran Sonnet-high on other 6-step puzzles: 97.5 against Opus-low's 98.75, at about half the cost. That comparison had no test.
user_framing_choices.why_it_matters: Read alone, Test 5 sounds like 'pay for the bigger model at low effort'. Next to Sonnet-high, that advice does not hold on cost. A reviewer will find it in our own files.
user_framing_choices.option_a: (Opus) Test 5 plus 'about 2.5 times as costly; Sonnet-medium is one level below Sonnet's default'. Sonnet-high's 97.5 against Opus-low's 98.75 on other puzzles, at about half the cost, 'bounds how far Test 5 generalises'.
user_framing_choices.option_b: (Fable) Present Test 5 as 'the one positive', worded as Opus-low doing better than Sonnet-medium, and say that Study 1b's own sweep undercuts its practical message, with exact intervals and costs. Fable also asks for a paired Sonnet-high against Opus-low comparison.
user_framing_choices.option_merged: Test 5 is confirmatory and declared. Opus-low was no worse than Sonnet-medium by more than 10 points (d +17.5 [+8.75, +27.5]; that the interval lies above zero is a descriptive note only), at 2.48 times the list cost per puzzle and 2.03 times per correct answer (exploratory ratios). Sonnet-medium is one level below Sonnet's default (high). In Study 1b's sweep (descriptive, different set, one try per item over 40 bases), Sonnet-high scored 97.5 [91.26, 99.70] at $0.0188 per answer against Opus-low's 98.75 [93.23, 99.97] at $0.0395 (0.477 of the cost; no paired interval). So Test 5 supports the accuracy half of 'bigger model, less thinking' against a below-default Sonnet. It supports neither the cost half nor the claim against Sonnet at its default. These sentences travel with Test 5 everywhere, and in Related Work Test 5 is never presented as confirming or refuting the vendor's published advice in general.
user_framing_choices.why: It takes Fable's exact intervals and costs and Opus's tier labels. Wording Test 5 as 'better than' is not a test result here, because the superiority check is only a sensitivity check in the locked plan. The two cost ratios carry an exploratory label because the analysis file labels that item 'exploratory, no test'. Fable's paired comparison cannot be built from Study 1, which had no Sonnet-high arm, but it can be built from Study 1b's 40 bases as a free exploratory check.

user_framing_choices.question: How Tests 1-4 are framed, given that the power model had forecast Test 2's outcome
user_framing_choices.background: Before the main run, the pinned power model, fitted to 20 six-step chain puzzles from the length sweep, gave Test 2 a 'worse by more than the margin' reading with probability 1.00 at 80 puzzles (spec Amendment 1 item 4). The spec itself calls this 'not a result'. Opus's review leaves it out. Fable's says Tests 1-4 'confirmed a measured expectation'.
user_framing_choices.why_it_matters: If the paper is silent, a reviewer reading the locked spec will ask why a forecast outcome is presented as news. If we overstate it, that is wrong too: the forecast covers Test 2 only, not Tests 1-4.
user_framing_choices.option_a: (Opus) No mention. Tests 1, 2 and 4 are act one's negatives, with the error-rate ratio beside every difference.
user_framing_choices.option_b: (Fable) Tests 1-4 confirmed a forecast, so their value lies in the measured gaps, curves and costs, not in the verdicts.
user_framing_choices.option_merged: One sentence beside Test 2: the pinned power model forecast this reading before the run, and the spec calls the forecast 'not a result'. Tests 1-4 are the scoped answer for medium-effort cheap designs. Their 'worse by more than 10 points' readings are the pre-registered three-way readings of unadjusted intervals, not Holm declarations. The weight goes on magnitude: the error ratio sits beside each difference (Test 2: 11.04 [4.75, unbounded]; Test 4: 12.33 [5.17, unbounded]; Test 1: undefined, because Opus-medium made 0 errors in 80, so its exact upper bound of 4.5% is given instead). The pre-registered near-ceiling label is shown beside Tests 1-2, set before the main-run data.
user_framing_choices.why: It discloses Fable's point at the scope the file supports (Test 2 only), keeps the pre-registered readings as the labels, and near the ceiling puts the size of the gap where it can be seen.

user_framing_choices.question: The title
user_framing_choices.background: The title is yours (the outline lists it under 'decisions only the user can make'). Opus offered five options and Fable offered headline phrases. The compiler narrowed these to three, each naming Claude 5.5 and the synthetic puzzles.
user_framing_choices.why_it_matters: The title is the claim most people read. A claim title must not imply that the lesson was itself pre-registered, that every comparison was at equal money (only Tests 1-3 and B2 were), or that the lesson holds beyond one synthetic family.
user_framing_choices.option_a: (Opus, neutral form) 'Bigger Model, More Thinking, or More Tries? Spending a Fixed Budget Across Claude 5.5 Models on Synthetic Ledger Puzzles'. Opus's other options were dropped: one attached 'Pre-Registered, Equal-Money' to a post hoc lesson, and one used 'Hold Up'.
user_framing_choices.option_b: (Fable phrasing) 'Buy Thinking Before Votes: Model Size, Thinking Effort and Sampling Under a Fixed Budget, for Claude 5.5 on Synthetic Multi-Step Puzzles'.
user_framing_choices.option_merged: (1) 'Effort First, Then Voting: Spending a Fixed Budget Across Claude 5.5 Models on Synthetic, Exact-Answer Multi-Step Puzzles'; (2) the Fable-phrased title above; (3) the neutral question title above.
user_framing_choices.recommendation: (1). If you prefer a title that makes no claim at all, (3).
user_framing_choices.why: (1) carries the message you already approved as a candidate (D-116) and the sentence the team chose, and its subtitle carries the scope. It keeps 'pre-registered' and 'equal-money' away from the claim. Its claim rests on Haiku 5.5 alone, so the abstract's first sentence must say so. (2) reads as purchase advice resting on one cheap model. (3) is the safest but tells the reader nothing about the answer.

user_framing_choices.question: The abstract's headline sentences
user_framing_choices.background: The abstract's opening sentences carry the main numbers. Fable's version describes the inconclusive single-try tests as 'within 2 to 8 points' and quotes 'a seventh' of the price, which the spec's fixed wording does not allow. Opus's version has a garbled scope phrase.
user_framing_choices.why_it_matters: The abstract is quoted and indexed, so every number in it must be exact and carry its tier.
user_framing_choices.option_a: (Opus) On exact-answer multi-step puzzles, raising Haiku 5.5's effort to max helped far more than any multi-call design at medium effort. At 16 steps a 6-try Haiku-max vote was no worse than one Opus-medium answer by more than 5 points, at about its price (B2). A single try, at about 1/6 to 1/10 of the cost, was non-inferior only at the secondary 10-point margin.
user_framing_choices.option_b: (Fable) Raising Haiku to max effort did what 40 default-effort votes, step splitting, a team and a judge could not. A single max-effort call came within a few points of Opus at a seventh to a tenth of the price, and a 6-vote at 89% of Opus's price was no worse by more than 5 points. (This wording breaks our rules for inconclusive tests and for the cost fraction.)
user_framing_choices.option_merged: Four sentences, each tiered. (1) Raising Haiku 5.5's thinking effort helped far more than buying more of its medium-effort tries (post hoc reading). (2) On 6-step puzzles, at no more than Opus-medium's price, a Haiku-medium vote was worse than one Opus-medium answer by more than 10 points (Tests 1-2). (3) On fresh 16-step puzzles, a 6-try Haiku-max vote was no worse than one Opus-medium answer by more than 5 points (d +0.63 [-1.15, +2.44]; B2, declared), at 0.894 of its price per answer. (4) A single Haiku-max try, at about 1/10 (6 steps) to 1/6 (16 steps) of the cost (k measured), was no worse than Opus-medium by more than 10 points, but we could not show it within 5 (B1, B3); its error rate was 3.4 times Opus-medium's at 16 steps [1.8, 10.1] and 6.8 times at 6 steps [1.7, unbounded]. A short scope sentence follows. Test 3 is left out.
user_framing_choices.recommendation: The merged option, including the error ratios.
user_framing_choices.why: It uses Opus's exact test wording and tiers and Fable's concrete price fraction. The error ratios show the size of the gap near the ceiling without replacing the pre-registered reading, which answers Fable's strongest point on magnitude.

user_framing_choices.question: How the cheap-judge part of the brief is answered
user_framing_choices.background: The original brief had a second question: can a cheap model be trusted as a judge? You dropped that study early, before Study 1 ran, to free budget (D-44). The only related data are one exploratory Haiku picker choosing among 8 Haiku-medium answers in the top-up, and the Haiku team's aggregator, which can overrule its helpers.
user_framing_choices.why_it_matters: A reader of the paper doesn't know the brief, but anyone who reads our public plans does. Saying nothing invites 'they hid it'. Saying too much invites 'one picker shows cheap judges fail'.
user_framing_choices.option_a: (Opus) One paragraph: the picker beat a single try, was not shown to beat a plain vote over the same 8, fell 19-25 points short of a perfect picker, and chose sample 1 in about half the puzzles (position effects not studied). The judge question stays largely open.
user_framing_choices.option_b: (Fable) The judge question is 'barely answered': even a perfect picker over 8 medium-effort answers caps at 87.5 / 86.25, below Opus, and the question should be asked again at max effort. Fable also says 'do not buy cheap judges' and calls the picker strongly biased toward the first position.
user_framing_choices.option_merged: The picker is reported with the other multi-call designs in the top-up section: 62.5 / 67.5; above a single try; not shown to differ from a plain vote over the same 8; below a perfect picker (87.5 / 86.25), with about 43-44% of that headroom closed (post hoc); sample 1 picked in 81 of 160 (position effects not studied). Even a perfect picker over those 8 answers stays below Opus-medium's 96.25 / 100. The aggregator's counts (15 right answers turned wrong and 7 wrong turned right on chains; 9 and 18 on pieces) are the second, indirect case. One short Limits paragraph says that the judge question was planned as its own study, left out before Study 1 ran, and remains open. A judge study, including judging max-effort answers, goes in future work. It is never in the title, the abstract headline or the one sentence.
user_framing_choices.why: It gives the reason the question is unanswered (D-44), which neither review cited. It keeps Fable's ceiling point and the idea of asking again at max effort, and it uses Opus's safe position wording. Fable's 'do not buy cheap judges' generalises from one picker.

user_framing_choices.question: How much of the journey goes in the main text
user_framing_choices.background: You left this to the team (D-121, item 4). The style sheet you approved (D-122) records the team's plan: only the turns that explain the method go in the main text, briefly, and the rest goes in the appendix. You asked for the task-family switch to be told as part of the research (D-81).
user_framing_choices.why_it_matters: Too much journey turns the paper into a diary. Too little hides the decisions that explain the method: why ledger puzzles, why 6 steps, why the marking rule changed, and why a second study exists.
user_framing_choices.option_a: (Opus) Name Deviations 1 and 2 at first use. Put one deviation table and one disclosure list in the appendix. Add a Method paragraph on how new analyses get in (the fixed scripts).
user_framing_choices.option_b: (Fable) Put the original-rule line in the main text beside Tests 3 and 5, and add a one-page timeline of locks, deviations and run windows.
user_framing_choices.option_merged: Main text, briefly: the task-family switch (D-81); Deviation 1 (24 to 6 steps, with the length picked by a Haiku-only rule); Deviation 2 (the marking rule, as one line beside Tests 3 and 5); the Haiku-max surprise leading to Study 1b, which is the story itself; Haiku-max's place as first to trim and the power forecast, which explain the framing; and one Method paragraph on the fixed scripts. Appendix: Fable's timeline table, Opus's deviation table and disclosure list, the exposed puzzles, the upload retries, run-rule changes, code used after the locks, the timing of the reporting definitions, the top-up's earlier start, and the full four-view tables.
user_framing_choices.why: It matches the plan already in the approved style sheet and your D-81 and D-90 rulings. The only additions to the main text are the two facts a reviewer needs to judge the framing: the cut order and the forecast.

user_framing_choices.question: Whether to add a 'buying guide' view for practitioners
user_framing_choices.background: The equal-money tests ask 'at the same money, is the cheap setup no worse than the bigger model by more than the margin?', not 'what is the cheapest way to reach a target accuracy?'. Both reviews suggest a buying guide. Your ruling D-94(5) dropped the fitted frontier (C6) because it was not fully defined before the data.
user_framing_choices.why_it_matters: Practitioners will read the paper for the second question. A figure that picks 'best buys' could read as a tested recommendation.
user_framing_choices.option_a: (Opus) An optional buying-guide figure per length, labelled post hoc by tier and study. It needs your ruling because C6 was dropped.
user_framing_choices.option_b: (Fable) A cost-for-target-accuracy table and frontier, 'the buying guide the brief asks for', plus costs per 10,000 puzzles.
user_framing_choices.option_merged: Say the one sentence above in the Introduction. Any buying-guide view is a post hoc reading on point estimates, labelled by tier and study, with nothing fitted. In Study 1b, at 12 and 16 steps the only non-Haiku setting is Opus-medium. The length sweep also ran Sonnet-medium and Opus-medium at those lengths on other sets (20 base puzzles, one try, not cost-matched). That correction fixes an error both reviews shared. The per-10,000-puzzle line is optional.
user_framing_choices.recommendation: Include the Introduction sentence. Do not draw a selected frontier. Instead, the main effort figure plots accuracy against cost per answer (log scale) for every measured setup at 6 and 16 steps, with tiers in the caption. The per-10,000-puzzle line goes in the Discussion with accuracies beside it.
user_framing_choices.why: This answers the buyer's question honestly without bringing back C6 or a pick that looks tested, and it keeps the paper simple for the reader (D-90).

must_not_claim: Never use 'matches', 'matched', 'as good as', 'level with', 'on par', 'Opus-level', 'can stand in for', 'closed the gap', 'reached Opus's range', 'about as high as' or 'measurably below'. Never reuse D-116's first wording, the outline's 'A Haiku-max vote held up', or the stamped headline_wording strings.
Never present 'effort first, then voting' as tested or pre-registered. It is our reading across two studies, not a test.

Never generalise the lesson to cheap models in general (only Haiku 5.5 was tested), or beyond one synthetic ledger family at 6-16 steps, Claude 5.5 models, short prompts and list prices of 2026-10-12/13.
Never say a Haiku-max vote reaches Opus-medium's accuracy 'for a fraction of the price'. B2 cost 0.894 of Opus-medium's price, and the cheaper votes are descriptive points with no paired interval.

Never call B1 or B3 'worse', 'within 2 to 8 points' or 'below' Opus-medium as a test result. Use the section 10 inconclusive template with error ratios; the interval below zero is only a labelled descriptive note.
Never say 'one-seventh'. The cost is always 'about 1/k of the cost per answer, k measured' (1/6 at 16 steps, 1/10 at 6), never one figure for both lengths.
Never say Opus-low 'beats' or is 'superior to' Sonnet-medium, or that Test 5 supports 'bigger model, less thinking' on cost or against Sonnet at its default.
Never say the power model forecast Tests 1-4. It forecast Test 2 only, and the spec calls it 'not a result'.
Never say the confirmatory family 'tested the wrong lever', or that all five Study 1 tests held every model at medium effort (Test 5 used Opus-low).
Never call Tests 1-4 or B1/B3 'declared' or 'Holm-controlled'. Holm declared only Test 5 in Study 1, and B2 at the primary margin in Study 1b. Never pool the studies.
Never present Test 3 as a clean negative, or say Tests 1-4 hold 'in every view'. Test 3 changes in two views.
Never present Test 4 as equal-money, and never write 'Test 4 at pieces'.
Never say Tests 1-2 ran 'at Opus-medium's price'. Test 1 spent 0.909 of it, so write 'at no more than'.
Never state D-125's second surprise causally ('Haiku repeats its wrong answers, so votes stall'). Write that the wrong answers often repeat and the votes level off; no cause is shown.
Never say 'no puzzle below 50% is rescued', 'more votes eventually hurt', or that a different temperature would lift the plateau.
Never say Study 1b or B3 'replicated' Study 1, and never call any one result 'the strongest'.
Never say cheap judges cannot be trusted, 'do not buy cheap judges', or that the picker has 'a strong position bias'. Never generalise to LLM-as-judge.
Never claim a crossover length between model size and effort, or say where Opus fails.
Never put 'Pre-Registered' or 'Equal-Money' next to a claim phrase in the title.
Never call Haiku-max votes the cheapest route at 12-16 steps. In Study 1b only Opus-medium was the alternative there, and the length sweep's Sonnet-medium points were not cost-matched.
Never say the Haiku-max gap to Opus-medium widens with length, or that 'accuracy follows tokens, not the effort label'.
Never recommend an 'odd-sized vote' as tested advice. B2 used k = 6, and the odd-size point is a post hoc note.
Never say 'voting does not work' in general. The negative is specific to medium-effort Haiku votes at Opus-medium's price on this family.
Never claim any Haiku-max latency result.
disclosures: Haiku-max x3 was an exploratory extra, listed first to trim in the budget plan (D-27), so raising the cheap model's effort was not among Study 1's tests.

Study 1b was designed after Study 1's results were opened: its margin, vote cap and length were chosen knowing the Haiku-max numbers. It used fresh, never-sent puzzles from the same generator, and lock 4 went public before its first call.
The pinned power model forecast Test 2's reading before the main run (spec Amendment 1 item 4), and the spec labels the forecast 'not a result'.
Sonnet ran one level below its default effort (high) in Tests 3 and 5.
Deviation 1 (24 to 6 steps) and Deviation 2 (the marking rule) are named where the tests are first reported, with one original-rule line beside Tests 3 and 5 and the full tables in the appendix.
The planned cheap-judge study (Study 5) was left out before Study 1 ran (D-44). The picker is the only direct related data.
The pre-registration itself uses 'matches' to mean non-inferiority within the margin (D-39 item 4; D-68 F3). The paper writes every such reading as 'no worse than X by more than N points'.
B2's accuracy is the expected accuracy of a 6-try vote, estimated from 10 tries per puzzle. Its per-shape costs (1.091 on chains, 0.733 on pieces) are given beside it.
The near-ceiling label beside Tests 1-2 was set from the length sweep, before the main-run data.
No drift check spans Study 1 and Study 1b. Every cross-study or cross-window comparison is our reading, not a test.
Temperature, top_p and top_k were never sent. The API returns an error for any temperature other than 1, so how alike the tries are is a property of the model.

AI use (D-129): AI tools were used under the authors' direction, and the statement names truthfully what they did. Anthropic had no role in the design, analysis or reporting. The models studied, the AI tools and the API credit are Anthropic's.

reviewer_risks.risk: The headline lesson is a post hoc reading that spans two studies with different puzzle sets and days
reviewer_risks.answer: Label it every time ('our reading, not a test'). Anchor the opening on two confirmatory tests (Tests 1-2 and B2). Give the within-study basis: in Study 1, on the same puzzles at about the same cost, one Haiku-max try scored 97.5 / 95.0 against 49.36 / 58.95 for a 4-try Haiku-medium vote (post hoc; exploratory arm). Say that no drift check links the studies.

reviewer_risks.risk: The pre-registered tests did not contain the lever that mattered
reviewer_risks.answer: Say so ourselves in the introduction (F-03), cite the budget plan's cut order, and show that the effort result became confirmatory only through a separate, publicly locked study on fresh puzzles.

reviewer_risks.risk: Test 5's practical message rests on a below-default Sonnet
reviewer_risks.answer: The Sonnet-default and Sonnet-high sentences travel with Test 5 everywhere (F-04). It supports only the accuracy half of 'bigger model, less thinking', and only against Sonnet-medium.

reviewer_risks.risk: Near-ceiling comparators make 5- and 10-point margins lenient
reviewer_risks.answer: Put the error ratio beside every difference (B1 3.4, B3 6.8, Test 2 11.04, Test 4 12.33; Test 1 undefined with an exact upper bound of 4.5%), use exact intervals where the bootstrap collapses, and say that the design cannot show where Opus fails.

reviewer_risks.risk: Test 2's outcome had been forecast, so the negatives look unsurprising
reviewer_risks.answer: Disclose the forecast at its true scope (Test 2 only, 'not a result') and put the weight on measured gaps, error ratios, vote curves and costs (F-05).

reviewer_risks.risk: Deviation 1 (moving to 6 steps) might have created the negative vote result
reviewer_risks.answer: At 24 steps Haiku-medium's single try scored 0.4% / 1.2% against Opus-medium's 96% / 88% (exploratory pilot), so a vote would not have come near there either. The 6-step length was picked by a Haiku-only rule, with the Opus and Sonnet ladder answers sealed (G2-12).

reviewer_risks.risk: Winner's curse: Study 1b was designed after seeing the surprise
reviewer_risks.answer: Fresh, never-sent sets, a public lock 4, k from cost-only rows, and B1/B3 reported plainly as inconclusive at 5 points. Never write 'replicated'.

reviewer_risks.risk: A claim title overstates a post hoc, one-family, one-cheap-model lesson
reviewer_risks.answer: Scope in the subtitle (Claude 5.5, synthetic puzzles), no 'pre-registered' or 'equal-money' beside the claim, and an abstract that names Haiku 5.5 in its first sentence. The neutral question title is the fallback.

reviewer_risks.risk: The brief's judge question looks dodged
reviewer_risks.answer: State that it was planned, left out before Study 1 (D-44) and remains open. Report the picker and aggregator only as exploratory cases, and list a judge study in future work.

include: The one sentence (F-01, team decision) as the abstract's last line and the conclusion's first line, with its label and scope.
The abstract per F-07, with the B1/B3 error ratios (F-21) and the scope sentence (F-20); Test 3 left out.

Introduction: the budget question, the effort-first answer, and the two confirmatory anchors (F-02); a 'what the pre-registered tests asked' paragraph (F-03 plus the power forecast, F-05); findings ordered per D-125; the equal-money sentence (F-24, corrected).

Study 1 results: Tests 1-2 with spend, the near-ceiling label and error ratios (F-15, G2-20, F-21); Test 3 with its marking-rule qualifier and the exploratory pieces counterpart (F-13, G1-01); Test 4 as a cheap baseline (F-14); Test 5 with the Sonnet sentences (F-04, corrected); the plateau description (F-17); the token finding as a smaller surprise (F-19).
Study 1b results: B2 with per-shape costs and 'estimated from 10 tries' (F-12); B1/B3 in the section 10 template (F-10, F-11); 're-tested', never 'replicated' (F-23).
Effort and length: Opus effort with the ceiling caveat (F-16); no widening gap with length (G2-23).
Top-up: the picker reported among the multi-call designs, with its headroom (G2-06), and the aggregator counts (G2-26).

Discussion: the within-study basis (F-18); the share of errors removed and the odd-vote-size note (G1-08, G1-09); Test 5 against the vendor's advice (G2-09); Sonnet-high's cost per correct answer (G2-08); the judge question left open (F-08); the brief's price-ratio question answered by item 9d ('no break-even within 40 samples' for the medium-effort vote against Opus-medium and Sonnet-medium; pre-specified descriptive); the per-10,000-puzzle line if you agree (G2-27).
Limits: the scope sentence (F-20); the corrected D-116 limit sentence (F-22); Sonnet below its default; temperature (G3-03); no cross-study drift check (G1-19).
Method: the fixed-scripts paragraph (F-25); the pre-registration's own use of 'matches' (G1-16); Deviations 1 and 2 at first use; the task-family switch (D-81).
Future work: a judge study, including judging max-effort answers (G1-29, judge part).

exclude.item: Fable headline options 2-6 (F-26, F-27, G1-31) and Fable's headline 1 as worded
exclude.reason: They break wording rules ('closes most of the gap', 'as accurate as', 'measurable gap' for inconclusive tests, 'beats') or are wrong in fact ('the same tokens', 'no puzzle below 50% is rescued', 'more than 40 points' on pieces, 'the one effort step not used'). F-07 carries the usable content.

exclude.item: The phrase 'tested the wrong lever'
exclude.reason: Too loaded, and Fable's supporting facts are wrong (Test 5 used Opus-low; B2 is confirmatory). The lesson is kept in plain words (F-03).

exclude.item: 'Odd-sized vote', '2-10x the cost per correct answer' and 'do not buy cheap judges' in the main message
exclude.reason: The one tested vote used k = 6, there is no single stamped 2-10x figure, and one picker cannot support a judge verdict.

exclude.item: Opus's 'Hold Up' title, and any title with 'Pre-Registered' or 'Equal-Money' beside a claim phrase
exclude.reason: 'Held up' is being replaced by B2's exact wording. The lesson is post hoc, and Tests 4, 5, B1 and B3 were not at equal money.

exclude.item: 'Picking helps on chains, re-working helps on pieces' (G3-06)
exclude.reason: The picker's chain gain over a plain vote has an interval that includes zero, and both arms are exploratory and cross-window.

exclude.item: A Study 1 'Opus-low vs Sonnet-high' analogue of Test 5 (G2-22)
exclude.reason: It cannot be computed, because Study 1 had no Sonnet-high arm. The paired check exists only on Study 1b's 40 bases.

exclude.item: A fitted or selected frontier ('best buys')
exclude.reason: C6 was dropped (D-94(5)). Any such view is a post hoc reading and could read as a tested recommendation.

user_framing_choices.question: The one sentence a reader should remember (and the main-message paragraph in the Discussion)
user_framing_choices.background: You left this to the team (D-121, item 6). The working candidate is 'effort first, then voting' (D-116, approved as a candidate). Its first summary used two phrases our wording rules now forbid, so it was reworded before use.
user_framing_choices.why_it_matters: It closes the abstract and opens the conclusion, and it is what readers repeat. If it says more than the data show (that it was tested, or that it holds for every cheap model), a reviewer will catch it.
user_framing_choices.option_a: (Opus) 'Effort first, then voting': raising Haiku 5.5's thinking effort to max helped far more than any multi-call design tried at medium effort; labelled as our reading across both studies, with the scope.
user_framing_choices.option_b: (Fable) 'Buy thinking before you buy votes': thinking first, then a small odd-sized vote of the thinking-heavy setting; buy the bigger model only for the last few points, at 2-10 times the cost per correct answer; do not buy default-effort samples, teams or cheap judges.
user_framing_choices.option_merged: Effort first, then voting: for the cheap model studied here (Haiku 5.5) on exact multi-step puzzles, raise its thinking effort before you buy more of its tries; the next step is a small vote of max-effort tries. (Our reading across both studies, not a test; one synthetic ledger family at 6-16 steps, Claude 5.5 models only, short prompts, list prices of 2026-10-12/13.) The Discussion opens with the longer main-message paragraph (claim C-102), each part carrying its tier.
user_framing_choices.recommendation: Team decision: the merged sentence, always with its 'our reading, not a test' label and scope; the Discussion paragraph as in C-102.
user_framing_choices.why: It keeps the D-116 label and adds Fable's plain 'raise it before you buy more'. It drops Fable's extras the files do not support: 'odd-sized' (the one tested vote used 6 tries), '2-10 times' (no single stamped figure) and 'do not buy cheap judges' (one picker; the judge study was dropped, D-44). Both halves have a basis: within Study 1, at about the same cost on the same puzzles, one Haiku-max try scored 97.5 / 95.0 against 49.36 / 58.95 for a 4-try Haiku-medium vote (post hoc, exploratory arm); in Study 1b a 6-try Haiku-max vote was no worse than one Opus-medium answer by more than 5 points (B2, confirmatory).

user_framing_choices.question: What the paper leads with
user_framing_choices.background: The current outline opens with 'Cheap votes lost'. Both reviews want the lead to move to effort. You ruled the three-part structure (Study 1, Study 1b, the top-up; D-116) and confirmed the story turns on the Haiku-max surprise, with two smaller surprises (D-125).
user_framing_choices.why_it_matters: The first paragraph decides what the reader thinks the paper is about. Negatives alone read as 'cheap models lose'; Haiku-max alone invites 'they found one good result after looking'.
user_framing_choices.option_a: (Opus) Lead with the budget question and 'effort first, then voting'; keep the three parts in study order; two acts (medium-effort cheap tries did not pay, then max effort changed the picture).
user_framing_choices.option_b: (Fable) Re-centre the whole paper on effort, voting and teams secondary, and open by admitting that the pre-registered part answered a narrower question than the brief.
user_framing_choices.option_merged: Abstract and Introduction open with the budget question and the effort-first answer (labelled our reading) plus two confirmatory anchors: Tests 1-2 (6 steps) and B2 (fresh 16-step puzzles); comparing the two anchors is descriptive (different studies, sets, days; no drift check links them). Introduction findings in order: (1) at medium effort cheap tries fell short (Tests 1-2 and 4, scoped); (2) the Haiku-max surprise and its fresh test (B2; B1 and B3 with error ratios and cost); (3) the two smaller surprises, worded without a cause (wrong answers often repeat and votes level off; Haiku-medium wrote about as many output tokens as Opus-medium, so the price gap stayed near the list ratio); (4) Test 5 with its Sonnet caveat; (5) the effort sweep; (6) the top-up designs (exploratory). The body keeps study order; the token finding stays out of the title and headline.
user_framing_choices.why: It follows D-116 and D-125, rests the opening on two confirmatory tests, labels the one cross-study reading, and gives the storyline (C) you chose for the voice. The repeat surprise is worded without 'so' because the data show repeats and the plateau together, not that one causes the other.

user_framing_choices.question: How candidly the paper says the confirmatory tests did not test the lever that mattered (the cheap model's own effort), and how the negatives are framed
user_framing_choices.background: Study 1's tests kept Haiku at medium effort (Tests 1-4 varied only votes and step splitting; Test 5 compared Opus-low with Sonnet-medium). Haiku-max was an exploratory extra, first to cut (D-27), and became a test only in Study 1b. Fable says the pre-registered part 'tested the wrong lever'; Opus tells it as the surprise. Two planning parts disagreed on placement (Introduction vs Discussion) and one treated this as already delegated to the team; it is routed to you because it shapes the story D-125 set.
user_framing_choices.why_it_matters: Anyone reading the public budget plan can see this, so saying it ourselves is stronger. But Fable's version has two factual errors (Test 5 used Opus-low, so not every test held effort at medium; B2 is confirmatory, so the answer did not come only from an exploratory arm), and Test 3 is not a clean negative.
user_framing_choices.option_a: (Opus) Tell it as a turn: at medium effort cheap tries did not pay; max effort changed the picture; the surprise became B1-B3 through a new lock on fresh puzzles.
user_framing_choices.option_b: (Fable) Say the confirmatory family tested the wrong lever: five tests at medium effort, four clean negatives under every view, the answer from an arm marked first to trim; a lesson about the design's assumptions.
user_framing_choices.option_merged: Introduction: one plain paragraph 'What the pre-registered tests asked' (claim C-125): the tests answered a narrower question than the brief; raising Haiku's effort was not among them; Haiku-max was an exploratory extra, first to trim, and led to Study 1b, a separate pre-registration whose B1-B3 are confirmatory; the effort contrast itself is descriptive. Discussion: one sentence naming the design-prior lesson, labelled our reading (C-112). Each negative scoped: Tests 1, 2 and 4 read the same in every pre-registered view; Test 3 is fragile and never grouped as a clean negative; Test 4 is a cheap baseline at 0.088 of Opus-medium's cost; Tests 1-2 ran at 'no more than' Opus-medium's price. No 'wrong lever', not in the title or abstract.
user_framing_choices.why: It keeps Fable's honest point in plain words, fixes its two errors using the rulings (D-27, D-96, D-98), and keeps the surprise as the turn (D-125). 'Wrong lever' is too loaded.

user_framing_choices.question: Does Test 3 appear in the abstract?
user_framing_choices.background: Test 3 (equal-money Haiku-medium vote against one Sonnet-medium answer, chains) reads 'worse by more than 10 points' under the marking rule as run, but inconclusive under the original rule (before Deviation 2, adopted after Sonnet's length-sweep replies were seen) and when copy slips are forgiven. Its pieces counterpart (exploratory) is also inconclusive.
user_framing_choices.why_it_matters: Abstract sentences get quoted without qualifiers; Test 3 is the one Study 1 reading that changes with the marking rule.
user_framing_choices.option_a: (Opus) Keep Test 3 out of the abstract; report it in Results with its qualifier.
user_framing_choices.option_b: Include Test 3 in the abstract with a short qualifier.
user_framing_choices.option_merged: The abstract names Tests 1-2 (and the Results name Test 4), which read the same under both marking rules; Test 3 appears in Results with its one-line qualifier and the exploratory pieces line; the four-view table goes in the appendix (D-90).
user_framing_choices.why: It keeps the abstract to readings that hold under both rules and follows your D-90 condition that the marking rule 'should not overcomplicate the reader'.

user_framing_choices.question: How Test 5 is framed beside the Sonnet-high result
user_framing_choices.background: Test 5 is Study 1's only Holm-declared result: Opus-low was no worse than Sonnet-medium by more than 10 points. Sonnet's default effort is high, so Study 1 ran it one level below default. Study 1b's sweep later ran Sonnet-high on other 6-step puzzles: 97.5 against Opus-low's 98.75, at under half the cost (no test).
user_framing_choices.why_it_matters: Read alone, Test 5 sounds like 'pay for the bigger model at low effort'. Next to Sonnet-high that advice does not hold on cost, and a reviewer will find it in our files.
user_framing_choices.option_a: (Opus) Test 5 plus its cost and the Sonnet-default caveat; Sonnet-high 'bounds' how far Test 5 generalises.
user_framing_choices.option_b: (Fable) Test 5 as 'the one positive', worded as Opus-low doing better; Study 1b's sweep 'undercuts' it; asks for a paired Sonnet-high against Opus-low comparison.
user_framing_choices.option_merged: No verb either way. Test 5 is confirmatory and declared (d +17.5 [+8.75, +27.5]; the interval above zero is a descriptive note), at 2.48 times the list cost per puzzle and 2.03 times per correct answer (exploratory ratios). Beside it, always: Sonnet-medium is one level below Sonnet's default; on Study 1b's other 6-step set Sonnet-high scored 97.5 [91.26, 99.70] at $0.0188 against Opus-low's 98.75 [93.23, 99.97] at $0.0395 (no paired interval; cross-study, descriptive). So Test 5 supports the accuracy half of 'bigger model, less thinking' against a below-default Sonnet, not the cost half nor the claim against Sonnet at its default. The paired Sonnet-high comparison on Study 1b's 40 bases is a free exploratory analysis.
user_framing_choices.why: Both verbs editorialise; the merged sentences are the checked facts with tiers kept apart. 'Better than' is not a test result here (superiority was only a sensitivity check).

user_framing_choices.question: How the pre-run power forecast for Test 2 is used
user_framing_choices.background: Before the main run, the pinned power model, fed the length sweep's measured inputs, forecast with probability 1.000 that Test 2 would read 'worse by more than the margin' (spec Amendment 1 item 4; the spec calls it a forecast, 'not a result'). Opus's review left it out; Fable stretched it to Tests 1-4.
user_framing_choices.why_it_matters: Silence invites 'why present a forecast outcome as news'; overstating it is wrong too (Test 2 only).

claims.text: Format compliance of the confirmatory single-call arms was 97.5-100% under the marking rule as run (D-76 with Deviation 2's repeated-line rule; pre-specified descriptive): Haiku-medium 98.6% (3,155 of 3,200) on chains and 99.7% (3,191 of 3,200) on pieces; Opus-medium and Sonnet-medium 97.5% (78 of 80) on chains and 100% on pieces; Opus-low 98.75% (79 of 80) and 100%. claims.text: Flag R (a pre-specified tuning-bias check, reporting definitions §4) did not fire. When two Haiku-medium tries slipped at the same step from the same input, they wrote the same balances in 89.2% of pairs on general steps [90% CI 83.0, 94.9; 11,972 pairs] and in 66.6% on the rule kinds tuned against Haiku [90% CI 59.4, 73.3; 25,082 pairs]. The flag fires only if the tuned-kind rate is at least twice the general one. That is the tilt it guards against: tuned kinds making Haiku's slips repeat, which would work against the vote. The data lean the other way. Slips on the tuned kinds repeat less per pair, though they supply more agreeing pairs because they slip more often.

Haiku-medium's step slips cluster on two 'look again' rule kinds (pre-specified descriptive, item 14; partly by design, since these kinds were added where Haiku slipped). On chains, repeat_fixed steps slipped 1,105 of 3,700 times (29.9%) and repick2 steps 621 of 2,766 (22.5%), against 728 of 12,470 (5.8%) on general steps. At max effort these rates were 1 of 282 (0.4%) and 3 of 210 (1.4%) on chains; on pieces, repick2 still gave 7 of Haiku-max's 11 placed slips.

claims.text: The pre-registered fairness check (D-67; exploratory, flag-based) did not fire. Its targeting index compares Haiku's slip-rate ratio (targeted rule kinds against general steps) with the same ratio for the comparison models; a value above 1 would mean the targeted kinds hit Haiku harder. It was 0.82, 90% CI [0.43, 1.37]. Targeted kinds were harder than general steps for Haiku (slip-rate ratio 4.03, 90% CI [3.23, 5.10]) and for Sonnet (5.37, 90% CI [3.09, 10.70]). Opus made 0 targeted-kind slips and 1 other slip in 948 placed steps, so, as the spec requires when Opus has too few slips, the comparison pools Opus and Sonnet; 38 of its 39 slips are Sonnet's, so it is in effect Haiku against Sonnet. The house-rule index cannot be assessed (0 exposed slips on the comparison side), and the interval cannot exclude a moderate excess targeting of Haiku (up to about 1.4 times).

When paying for Opus, more effort bought no accuracy gain that these data could detect. In Study 1 (keep-list C10, exploratory), Opus-low minus Opus-medium was +1.25 [-3.75, +7.5] on chains and 0.0 on pieces (both 100; exact interval per C-005's rule), at $0.0037 / $0.0033 less per puzzle (about 7-9%). Opus is near the ceiling, so the data cannot separate 'effort does not help Opus' from 'these puzzles are too easy for Opus'.

claims.text: In paired Study 1 data (keep-list C10, exploratory), Haiku-low scored 4.5 points below Haiku-medium on both shapes (chains -4.5 [-6.91, -2.13]; pieces -4.5 [-7.84, -1.09]) for about 6% lower cost per puzzle. The rewording check moved Haiku-medium's level by +8.75 [0.0, +17.25]. It ran on Haiku-medium only, so whether a gap of this size between weak settings survives a rewording was not checked.

Haiku with thinking off (exploratory arm; medium effort with thinking disabled) scored 22.0 [16.97, 27.31] on chains and 23.5 [18.8, 28.6] on pieces, against Haiku-medium's 43.72 / 51.0, and saved about 19% / 12.5% of the cost per puzzle. The reply format asks only for the value after each step and a numbered final answer, with no worked reasoning (D-31), so this arm measures answering in that format with thinking disabled. On chains, 18.3% of its replies also failed the format (the format flag fires); scored on the final answer alone, it reached 28.0 instead of the official 22.0. So, by this arithmetic, format failures account for part of the chain shortfall. The design allows thinking to be disabled on Haiku only (at high effort or below), so there is no Sonnet or Opus counterpart.

At their own equal-money vote sizes (item 10; exploratory, no Holm, no verdict), the weaker Haiku settings also stayed far below one Opus-medium answer. Haiku-low's vote (39 tries on chains; 40 on pieces, capped from 46) scored 49.375 and 62.5: d -46.875 (95% interval -58.125 to -35.625) and -37.5 (-48.125 to -27.5). Haiku thinking-off's vote (40 tries, capped from 45 and 50) scored 42.75 and 40.0: d -53.5 (-64.375 to -42.0) and -60.0 (-70.0 to -48.75). Turning thinking off saved money per call but raised the cost per correct answer, from $0.0025 to $0.0040 on chains and from $0.0021 to $0.0041 on pieces (list price).

claims.section: Results: Study 1 (the Haiku-max surprise; one line also beside Tests 1-2)
claims.text: Haiku-max surprise (Study 1, exploratory; 3 tries per puzzle; no Holm, no verdict). A single Haiku-max try scored 97.5 [95.42, 99.17] on chains and 95.0 [91.25, 97.92] on pieces, at 0.109 and 0.085 of Opus-medium's list cost per puzzle. On chains, Opus-medium's 96.25 includes 2 extra-line format slips; its final-answer score is 98.75. A 3-try vote (capped by the 3 tries drawn, so not an equal-money vote; the equal-money vote size would have been 9 on chains and 11 on pieces) scored 100 and 98.75, at 0.328 and 0.254 of Opus's price. Paired differences against Opus-medium (exploratory, descriptive): +3.75 [+1.25, +10.0] on chains and -1.25 [-7.5, 0.0] on pieces. The arm generated the hypothesis that Study 1b then tested. On Study 1b's fresh 6-step set, Haiku-max scored 97.25 on chains and 94.25 on pieces per try (cross-study, descriptive).

claims.section: Results: Study 1 (post hoc reading; restated in the Discussion as the within-study anchor)
claims.text: Post hoc reading of Study 1 (Haiku-max is an exploratory arm; no paired interval was computed). One Haiku-max try ($0.00441 chains, $0.00407 pieces) costs about as much as 4 Haiku-medium tries ($0.00440; about $0.00437). On the same puzzles, the single Haiku-max try scored 97.5 / 95.0 against 49.36 / about 58.95 for a 4-try Haiku-medium vote. Voting at medium effort added about 15 points for 36-40 tries' worth of money; going from medium to max added 44-54 points for about 4 times the money. 'Effort first, then voting' is a reading across the two studies, not a test; this is its within-study anchor.

Per-piece view (D-23, item 7; secondary descriptive). On the pieces shape, a single Haiku-medium try got 89.5% [87.8, 91.2] of single steps right, at $0.000182 per task (about 1/44 of Opus-medium's $0.00802). Haiku-max got 99.0% [98.3, 99.6] at $0.000678 (about 1/12); Opus-medium and Opus-low got 100%. A 40-vote per piece reached 93.75% [91.5, 95.7] at $0.00729 per task. The whole-answer pieces score is close to the per-piece rate compounded six times (0.895^6 = 0.51 against an observed 51.0; post hoc arithmetic).

claims.section: Results: Study 1 (restated in Discussion and limits)
claims.text: A same-meaning rewording of the prompt's opening and closing paragraphs (D-42(a): a robustness arm ruled in the plan, outside the confirmatory family; no test) raised Haiku-medium's single-try score by +8.75 points [0.0, +17.25] pooled on 40 fixed puzzles (20 bases x 2 shapes, 10 tries each; chains +11.5 [0.0, +23.5]; pieces +6.0 [-5.0, +17.0]). Haiku-medium's score may depend partly on wording: the data fit anything from no change to about +17. The size is comparable to the gain from a vote of 5 to 8 tries on chains (+7.0 at 5 tries, +9.3 at 8; descriptive), and small beside the gaps in Tests 1, 2 and 4 (33-43 points). Test 3, whose interval's upper end (-12.20) lies closest to the -10 margin, is the most exposed. The rewording was checked only on single Haiku-medium tries, not on votes, and never at max effort. On the 20 chain puzzles, the reworded prompt's replies were 100% format-compliant against 98.5% for main-run samples 1-10, so at most about 1.5 of the +11.5-point chain gain could come from format.

claims.text: The escalate-to-Opus cascade on Haiku-medium votes (item 9e; a pre-specified exploratory offline simulation). It takes a vote of the first k_c Haiku-medium tries (k_c = 5, 10 or 20); if the winning answer's share of that vote is below a threshold tau, it uses Opus-medium's answer instead. Each threshold was chosen on the odd-numbered base puzzles and scored on the 40 even-numbered ones. At k_c = 10 it saved nothing measurable on chains and traded 7.5 points for a 25% saving on pieces. Chains (tau 0.8): 90.0 vs Opus-medium's 92.5 on the same bases, d -2.5 [-7.5, 0.0], escalating 70% of puzzles, at $0.0408 vs $0.0416 (cost difference -0.0008 [-0.0072, +0.0049], spanning zero). Pieces (tau 0.7): 92.5 vs 100, d -7.5 [-15.0, 0.0], escalating 52.5%, at $0.0366 vs $0.0489 (25% cheaper; cost difference -0.0122 [-0.0195, -0.0047]). At k_c = 5 the accuracy loss was larger (chains -10.0 [-20.0, -2.5]; pieces -12.5 [-22.5, -2.5]). A cascade on Haiku-max tries was not simulated.

Shape (six one-step pieces vs one six-step chain; pre-specified descriptive, keep-list C2, C3, C5). In Study 1 at 6 steps, every arm's pieces-minus-chains interval included zero (Opus-low's and Opus-medium's start at zero): Haiku-medium +7.28 [-1.47, +15.38], Haiku-low +7.28 [-0.94, +15.16], Opus-medium +3.75 [0.0, +8.75], Sonnet-medium -5.0 [-18.75, +8.75] and Haiku-max -2.5 [-6.25, +0.83]. For Tests 1-2, the vote's gap to Opus-medium was not shown to differ between shapes (C5: +4.52 [-9.85, +18.23]). In the length sweep (20 bases each, one try), Sonnet-medium scored higher on chains than on pieces at 4 of 5 lengths (6, 8, 12 and 16 steps). In Study 1b, Haiku-max scored lower on pieces than on chains at 6 steps (94.25 vs 97.25; its gap to Opus-medium was -5.75 on pieces vs -1.5 on chains), but higher on pieces at 12 steps (95.125 vs 90.375) and at 16 steps (93.0 vs 92.25). The shape effect did not keep one direction across sets and lengths.

claims.section: Results: Study 1 (appendix; one Method clause 'measured in Batch')
claims.text: All headline accuracy results were measured in Batch. In the 10-puzzle real-time subset (pre-specified descriptive, item 6; no test), accuracy was lower in real time than in Batch for all three models (real time vs Batch): Haiku-medium 0.54 vs 0.58 over 50 calls; Opus-medium 0.9 vs 1.0 and Sonnet-medium 0.7 vs 0.9 over 10 calls each (gaps of one and two answers). Output tokens were within about 1-7%. Pilot 1's real-time check (exploratory; 24 steps, 5 base puzzles in both shapes, original marking rule) pointed in mixed directions: Opus-medium chains 100% in real time against 60% in Batch (5 tries each; pieces 100% in both), Sonnet-medium pieces 20% against 40% and chains 40% against 20%, Haiku-medium 0% whole answer in both (79.2% against 81.1% per piece). The subsets are far too small to tell whether there is a real difference in either direction.

The pre-specified low-information flag did not fire: Haiku-medium scored 51.0% on pieces (the flag fires if its single-try score on pieces is above 60%; reporting definitions item 5). Haiku-medium's per-puzzle single-try scores spread to both ends: on chains, 16 of 80 puzzles were below 10% and 11 at 90% or more. The median over puzzles was 40.0 on chains and 50.0 on pieces.

claims.section: Results: Study 1b (opening; briefly, as a turn that explains the method)
claims.text: Study 1b was designed after Study 1's results were opened: its 5-point margin, vote cap of 10 and 16-step length were chosen knowing Study 1's Haiku-max numbers (D-96). Its test sets were generated and frozen before any Haiku-max data existed (Study 1's unused candidate and reserve sets), were never sent to any model under test, and were never attempted by a free helper; the never-sent record covers 3 sets and 400 items. It ran under its own publicly timestamped lock, with k taken from cost-only rows. The sets come from the same generator and preset family (ledger-0.5, l14 rules), so B1-B3 re-test the Haiku-max idea on fresh puzzles of the same task family; they show nothing about other task types and are not evidence of generality.
