claims.text: B2 (Study 1b, confirmatory; the only Study 1b test declared under Holm at the 5-point primary margin). On fresh 16-step procedures, the expected accuracy of a 6-try Haiku-max vote (estimated from 10 tries per item) was no worse than one Opus-medium answer by more than 5 points: d +0.63 points, 95% interval -1.15 to +2.44; p = 0.0001, below its Holm threshold of 0.0083. It came at about Opus-medium's price per answer (k = 6 measured; list cost $0.0670 vs $0.0750, ratio 0.894). Per shape, the vote cost 1.091 times Opus-medium's price on chains (more than Opus) and 0.733 on pieces. Accuracy 98.44 vs 97.81; error ratio 0.71 [0.24, 2.11]. The reading is the same in all three views and in the sensitivity check that drops the one base puzzle in B2's set whose answer key appeared in a helper work session (+0.64 [-1.20, +2.50], 79 bases). B2 shows 'no worse by more than 5 points' at about equal money; it is neither a saving nor superiority: its interval includes zero, although the 5- and 6-try votes scored higher on point estimate.

B1 (Study 1b, confirmatory; Holm within Study 1b): at 16 steps we could not show that a single Haiku-max try is within 5 points of Opus-medium (d -5.19 points, 95% interval -7.75 to -2.69; p = 0.566). Its error rate was 3.4 times Opus's (95% interval 1.8 to 10.1). (Descriptive, not a pre-registered test: the whole 95% interval lies below zero.) At the secondary 10-point margin, it was no worse than Opus-medium by more than 10 points (p = 0.00027). One try costs about 1/6 of Opus-medium's per answer (k measured; the measured ratio is 6.71). Accuracy 92.625 vs 97.8125.

claims.text: B3 (Study 1b, confirmatory; 6 steps, 40 bases): we could not show that a single Haiku-max try is within 5 points of Opus-medium (d -3.63, 95% interval -7.0 to -1.5; p = 0.206). Its error rate was 6.8 times Opus's (95% interval 1.7 to unbounded; Opus-medium made 1 error in 160 tries). (Descriptive, not a pre-registered test: the whole interval lies below zero.) At the secondary 10-point margin, it was no worse than Opus-medium by more than 10 points (p = 0.0011). It costs about 1/10 of Opus-medium's per answer (k measured). Accuracy 95.75 vs 99.375. The cost fraction differs between the two lengths (and sets), so one figure is never quoted for both.

The pre-registered sensitivity that leaves out the base puzzles whose answer keys appeared in a helper work session (one in the 16-step set, two in the 6-step set; 79, 79 and 38 bases) gives the same readings for all three tests in all three views: B1 d -5.19 (95% interval -7.85 to -2.66), inconclusive at 5 points and no worse than Opus-medium by more than 10 (p = 0.00014); B2 +0.64 (-1.20 to +2.50), no worse by more than 5; B3 -3.82 (-7.50 to -1.45), inconclusive at 5 and no worse by more than 10 (p = 0.0016). The descriptive outputs were not re-run without them.

Study 1b's locked power table (spec §5) said in advance that, near Opus's ceiling, a 5-point margin confirms 'no worse' only if Haiku-max's true accuracy is close to Opus's. With Opus at 98% (Holm's strictest step), B1's chance of reading 'no worse by more than 5 points' was 0.89-0.99 if Haiku-max were at 98%, 0.23-0.31 at 95% and 0.00-0.01 at 92%. Haiku-max scored 92.625 at 16 steps, so an inconclusive B1 was the expected outcome for a gap of this size; the error-rate ratio beside the test carries the size of the gap.

Haiku's chains kept the format in 375 of 400 replies at low and at high (the about-5% flag fires, 6.25%), 381 of 400 at medium (plus 1 truncation), 390 of 400 at xhigh and 796 of 800 at max; its pieces were 400 of 400 at low to xhigh and 799 of 800 at max (thinking-off: 112 and 313 of 400). claims.section: Discussion and limits (opens the Discussion; the one sentence is C-128)
claims.text: Main message (our reading across both studies, not a test; each part keeps its own tier; the studies differ in puzzle sets, lengths and days, and no drift check links them): effort first, then voting. On one synthetic family of exact multi-step puzzles, raising Haiku 5.5's effort to max helped far more than any multi-call design tried at medium effort. At no more than Opus-medium's price, medium-effort Haiku votes were worse than one Opus-medium answer by more than the 10-point margin (Tests 1-2, confirmatory; pre-registered three-way readings of unadjusted intervals, not Holm-declared). So was step voting, at about 1/11 of the cost (Test 4, same reading). The Haiku team stayed 27.5-43.75 points below Opus-medium. The Haiku picker's 62.5 / 67.5 sat about 33 points below Opus-medium's 96.25 / 100 (both exploratory and across run windows, same-model flag not fired; the picker gap is arithmetic, with no interval). We could not show that a single Haiku-max try is within 5 points of Opus-medium (B1 at 16 steps, B3 at 6 steps; confirmatory, inconclusive at the primary margin). Its error rate was 3.4 and 6.8 times Opus-medium's, at about 1/6 (16 steps) and 1/10 (6 steps) of the cost per answer (k measured). At the secondary 10-point margin it was no worse than Opus-medium by more than 10 points. At 16 steps, the expected accuracy of a 6-try Haiku-max vote was no worse than one Opus-medium answer by more than 5 points (B2, confirmatory, declared under Holm), at about its price (0.894 pooled; 1.091 on chains, 0.733 on pieces).

claims.text: Tuning bias runs both ways. The rule kinds were developed on Haiku's slips, which works against the Haiku vote; other choices work for it: the 10-point margin, refusals and truncations counted as wrong, and a 25-50% difficulty band where voting helps most. In the plan's words, 'the net direction is not known in advance'. The pre-registered fairness check (exploratory, flag-based) gave a targeting index of 0.82 (90% interval 0.43 to 1.37; 1 means no extra targeting), and its flag did not fire; but Opus slipped once in 948 placed steps, so the comparison side is in effect Sonnet, the house-rule index could not be assessed, and the interval cannot exclude the tuned kinds targeting Haiku up to about 37% more than the comparison models. A second pre-registered check (flag R) did not fire: when two Haiku-medium tries slipped at the same step from the same input, they wrote identical balances in 66.6% of pairs on the tuned kinds against 89.2% on general steps, the reverse of the worry that tuning made Haiku's wrong answers more alike. The checks bound the tuning bias; they do not remove it.

claims.text: Practical rules (a post hoc synthesis for Haiku 5.5 on this puzzle family; our reading, not a test; each step keeps its own tier). (1) For Haiku 5.5, raise thinking to max before paying for a bigger model. The confirmatory part: B1 (16 steps) and B3 (6 steps) were no worse than Opus-medium by more than the secondary 10-point margin, at about 1/6 and 1/10 of the cost per answer (k measured). We could not show them within 5 points, and a single Haiku-max try made 3.4 and 6.8 times Opus-medium's errors. (2) Many medium-effort Haiku calls did not buy Opus-medium's accuracy. At no more than its price the votes were worse by more than 10 points (Tests 1-2, unadjusted three-way readings). Step voting, at about 1/11 of the price, also fell short (Test 4, a cheap baseline, not an equal-money result). The top-up arms are exploratory. (3) If you need accuracy no worse than Opus-medium's by more than 5 points at about its price, vote a few max-effort Haiku tries, and work out the equal-money vote size for your own task and shape (B2: 6 Haiku-max tries at 16 steps, 0.894 of Opus's price pooled, but 1.091 on chains and 0.733 on pieces). (4) When paying for a bigger model, use low or medium effort for Opus and the default (high) for Sonnet, and do not assume the top effort levels help (measured at 6 steps only). (5) Any frontier or buying guide is a post hoc reading on point estimates (the fitted frontier was dropped before the data), labelled by tier and study.

claims.text: Practical advice never puts Opus-medium on a 'drop' list: on fresh puzzles it scored above a single Haiku-max try on point estimate in B1 (97.81% against 92.63%) and B3 (99.38% against 95.75%).

The project's second question, whether cheap models can be trusted as judges, stays largely open: the planned judge study was left out of the project before Study 1 ran. The only direct data is one exploratory picker: Haiku-medium choosing among 8 of Haiku-medium's own main-run answers, shown in a fixed order. Nothing here tests grading a single answer, a stronger judge or judging max-effort answers; the paper does not generalise to LLM-as-judge, and a judge study, including judging max-effort answers, is future work.

must_not_claim: Barred words for any result: 'matches', 'matched' (including compounds such as 'budget-matched', 'money-matched', 'token-matched', 'the matched design'), 'equals', 'as good as', 'level with', 'on par', 'Opus-level', 'can stand in for', 'about as high as', 'closed the gap', 'reached Opus's range', 'measurably below', 'proves'; 'confirms' for an exploratory result or our reading. Non-inferiority is always 'no worse than X by more than N points' with d and its 95% interval (B2, Test 5 and the 5- and 6-try point estimates included).

D-116's first wording ('reached Opus-level accuracy', 'closed the gap', 'a small vote closed the gap'), the outline's 'A Haiku-max vote held up', NOW.md's old 'level with Opus on chains', and 'votes were tested only at medium effort' (plain Haiku-max votes ran).

Copying stamped texts: confirmatory.headline_wording and original_repeat_rule_appendix wording, test4_pieces.methods_note, groupc's 'definition fixed and timestamped before the data', the fairness 'pilot scale' reason; the locked texts' 'matches' appears only as a marked quotation.
Calling Tests 1-4, or B1/B3 at the 5-point margin, 'declared' or 'Holm-controlled'; writing 'Holm p = 0.0001' (write 'p = 0.0001, below its Holm threshold of 0.0083'); pooling Study 1 with Study 1b.
Test 3 as a clean negative, 'only under Deviation 2', or Tests 1-4 holding 'in every view'; Test 3's 'worse' reading extending to pieces.

For B1 and B3: 'worse', 'measurably/reliably/significantly/statistically worse', 'measurably below', 'came within', 'within 2 to 8 points', or any test-result wording beyond the spec section 10 template; never without the error ratio beside d.
'One-seventh' or '1/7' of the price; one cost fraction for both lengths (it is about 1/6 at 16 steps and 1/10 at 6, k measured).

B2 as a saving, superiority, 'beat', 'outperformed', 'better than', or a vote no worse than Opus-medium 'for a fraction of the price' (B2 cost 0.894 pooled, 1.091 on chains); B2 as six separately run votes.
Any post hoc k (for example vote@3 at 45% of the price) as a saving; report every k, not only the smallest that clears -5 (Study 1b pre-registered 'k-sensitivity: none').
Study 1b or B3 'replicated' or 'confirmed' Study 1; generality beyond this generator and preset family; 'never seen' for the test puzzles; any result as 'the strongest'.
The chain vote dip as 'falls', 'declines' or 'more votes hurt'.

Causal plateau claims: 'voting fails because errors repeat', 'Haiku repeats its wrong answers, so votes stall' in causal form, 'this mechanism explains Tests 1-3', 'no puzzle below 50% is rescued'; 'repetition is only weakly related to difficulty' on chains.
'Haiku-max's errors rarely/don't repeat' or any mechanism for B2 (no Haiku-max repeat share exists until the free analysis runs; even then describe only).
'Voting does not work' in general; the negative is specific to medium-effort Haiku votes at no more than Opus-medium's price on this family.
That a different temperature would lift the medium-effort plateau.
Haiku-max votes as 'the cheapest route among all options at 12-16 steps'; 'Sonnet (or Opus-low) was run only at 6 steps' without 'in Study 1b'.
That the Haiku-max gap to Opus-medium widens with length; the Opus-medium/Haiku-max price ratio as one number or extrapolated beyond 16 steps.

For Opus effort: 'flat', 'Opus-high is worse', 'the Opus dip', 'Opus effort is irrelevant', 'Opus-low is as good as Opus-max', 'Opus-high's 96.25% is one miss' (it is 3), or any order among effort points whose intervals overlap; write '96.25-100, not rising steadily with effort'.
'Accuracy follows tokens, not the effort label'; 'Haiku's accuracy rose with effort in every shape' (pooled points only).
Thinking-off at 16 steps as 'mostly format failure'; 'Haiku cannot reason without thinking'; any cross-model 'thinking off' comparison.

Compounding as a finding ('chains compound faster than independent steps', 'exactly compounded', 'compounding cannot explain it'); q as fitted or as pooled over both shapes; 'Sonnet does better on chains' in general or 'beats what compounding predicts'; 'pieces are the easier, vote-friendly shape' without naming model and effort.
'Claude Code beats the API'; Haiku-max's per-piece score as evidence about that gap; 'the surface matters as much as the model'.
For the picker: 'mostly chose', 'strong position bias', 'position-biased'; that it beat vote@8 (both intervals include 0); 'picking helps on chains, re-working helps on pieces'.
'Cheap models cannot be trusted as judges', 'do not buy cheap judges', 'the project's only cheap-judge data', or any generalisation to LLM-as-judge.
'Test 4 at pieces' as a name in prose while E-06 is open (write 'step voting on pieces (C13), the pieces counterpart of Test 4'); the C13 reading as 'confirmed'.

Test 4 as an equal-money result; any claim about decomposition at Opus-medium's budget or on tasks whose steps are not given; citing the spec's 'H2 cannot fail on dollars' in Test 4's defence; 'about 13 draws per step' at Opus's budget (it is about 25).
'Teams lose', E2 'level with step voting', or E2 against E3 as like for like; that the aggregator explains the team's lead; the chain aggregator counts without the pieces counts.
Any Study 1 vs Study 1b, cross-set or top-up vs main-run comparison as a test, an effect or 'confirmed'.
That the 5-try vote latency was measured or that a parallel vote was run; any latency result for Haiku-max.
Extending the vote results to other lengths (no equal-money Haiku-medium vote ran outside 6 steps); 'pre-registered at 6 steps' without Deviation 1.
That the 24-to-6-step move was chosen after seeing the length sweep's Opus or Sonnet answers, or that the N pick was blind to Pilot 1's Opus and Sonnet results (it was blind to the length sweep's).

Test 5: that it says anything about Sonnet at its default; 'a bigger model at low effort beats a mid model at its default'; that it supports the cost half of 'bigger model, less thinking'; that it confirms or refutes the vendor's 'cheaper per task' advice in general; 'Opus-low beats/is superior to Sonnet-medium'; 'Sonnet-high is cheaper than Opus-low at about the same accuracy' as a tested result; 'Test 5 could reverse'; a computed Study 1 Opus-low vs Sonnet-high analogue (Study 1 ran no Sonnet-high).
That the power model forecast Tests 1-4 (it forecast Test 2 only, 'not a result').
'Tested the wrong lever'; that all five Study 1 tests held every model at medium effort (Test 5 used Opus-low).
That Tests 1-2 ran 'at Opus-medium's price' (write 'at no more than'; Test 1 spent 0.909).
The 'verbosity tax' refutation beyond medium effort; 'the 40x gap shrinks to 3-11x because Haiku is verbose' at medium effort.
Choosing setups by cost per correct answer alone.
Any frontier or buying guide as pre-registered, fitted, or replacing C6.
'Effort first, then voting' as tested or pre-registered, or as holding for cheap models in general (only Haiku 5.5 was tested); 'odd-sized vote' as tested advice (B2 used k = 6).
'Batch and real time give the same answers'.
'The model was unchanged'; 'no drift between Study 1 and Study 1b'; 'guards against drift within Study 1' (the same-model check covers only the top-up window).
'The tuning works against the cheap side' or 'the vote's best case' stated alone; 'the fairness check removes the tuning bias'.
'Haiku's score depends on wording'; '+/-10 points of wording uncertainty'; small paired differences as 'within wording noise'.
'The ledger avoids the filter', 'refusals vanished', 'silent fallback'.

Process wording: 'to the cent' (write 'within one cent'); 'stamped before the data' or 'before the data' for Study 1's analysis code (write 'before any result was opened'); 'before any grading' for k (write 'before any score was seen'); 'pre-registered' for the reporting definitions (write 'fixed after lock 3, before any result was opened'); 'the main run used only locked code'; 'independent' for the AI sessions' separation or re-runs; 'before any data' for the near-ceiling label (write 'set before the main-run data').
Opus-medium on a 'drop' list.
'Only Sonnet moved' under Deviation 2 (write 'only Sonnet-medium's chain whole-answer accuracy moved').
That caching was ignored (the cached view changes no reading; headline costs stay uncached list prices).

A multiplicity-corrected reading of Tests 1-4 before it is computed with a correction fixed in advance; the cascade as 'the most promising route'; any pre-judged result for a free analysis not yet run.
'Pre-Registered' or 'Equal-Money' next to a claim phrase in the title.
Personal details: the remaining or unspent credit, the chats' names, personal reasons for pauses, battery or connection details (D-121(8)).
That Anthropic sponsored, endorsed or had any role in the study, or wording that understates what the AI tools did (D-129).

reviewer_risks.risk: The headline lesson is a post hoc reading spanning two studies with different puzzle sets and days, with no drift check between them
reviewer_risks.answer: Label it every time ('our reading, not a test'); anchor the opening on two confirmatory tests (Tests 1-2, B2); give the within-study basis (one Haiku-max try 97.5 / 95.0 against 49.36 / 58.95 for a 4-try Haiku-medium vote at about the same cost; post hoc, exploratory arm); add the free same-puzzle effort-against-samples analysis; say that no drift check links the studies.

reviewer_risks.risk: The pre-registered tests did not contain the lever that mattered (the cheap model's own effort)
reviewer_risks.answer: Say so ourselves in the Introduction (C-125), cite the budget plan's cut order, and show the effort result became confirmatory only through a separate, publicly locked study on fresh puzzles.

reviewer_risks.risk: One synthetic task family, with rule kinds developed on Haiku's own slips
reviewer_risks.answer: Scope the title, abstract and every claim to this family; present a case study plus a reusable equal-money protocol; give the two-sided bias table and its checks; name the dropped code family and the unrun ArXivMath check as future work.

reviewer_risks.risk: One vendor's models, studied with that vendor's AI tools and paid with its credit
reviewer_risks.answer: Mechanical exact scoring by locked code, no LLM judge; public timestamps on locks 1-4; byte-identical re-runs; costs agreed with the Console within one cent; AI-use statement per D-129; separation between AI sessions never called 'independent'.

reviewer_risks.risk: Study 1's Sonnet comparator ran one level below its default effort, which colours Tests 3 and 5
reviewer_risks.answer: Say so beside Tests 3 and 5 and every Opus-versus-Sonnet cost comparison; Opus-low was also below its default; Test 5 supports only the accuracy half of 'bigger model, less thinking'; show Study 1b's Sonnet-high point as a labelled cross-study reading, plus the free paired analysis on Study 1b's 40 bases.

reviewer_risks.risk: Near-ceiling comparator and lenient margins (B1 and B3 pass the 10-point margin with 3.4 and 6.8 times Opus-medium's errors; B2's 5-point margin chosen after Study 1)
reviewer_risks.answer: Error ratio beside every d; exact bounds where intervals collapse at 100%; say why the margins are 10 and 5; B1's errors are wrong states, not format; report the near-ceiling label; say the design cannot show where Opus-medium pulls ahead.

reviewer_risks.risk: Forking paths: many post hoc analyses added after the results were opened
reviewer_risks.answer: Each is labelled post hoc or exploratory, gets no verdict, runs as its own hash-checked script with its own result file; the appendix lists every estimate with its tier and the total count; where k is chosen, all k are reported.

reviewer_risks.risk: Novelty: majority voting, voting plateaus and multi-agent results at equal tokens are known
reviewer_risks.answer: Add Related Work; use the term cost-of-pass; say which known effects our data echo; state that the team and step-voting arms were not run at equal money or equal tokens; claim novelty narrowly.

reviewer_risks.risk: Winner's curse: the Haiku-max idea came from an exploratory arm, and Study 1b's margin, cap and length were chosen after Study 1's results were opened
reviewer_risks.answer: Study 1b used 400 never-sent puzzles frozen before any Haiku-max data, a publicly timestamped lock, k from cost-only rows; B1 and B3 reported plainly as inconclusive at 5 points, which the locked power table expected; write 're-tested on fresh puzzles', never 'replicated'.

reviewer_risks.risk: No latency data for the recommended setting (Haiku-max); the 5-try vote time is computed
reviewer_risks.answer: State the limit; give medium-effort medians and the computed vote times as computed; give the thinking-token proxy labelled as our reading; no Haiku-max latency claim; a paid check is not crucial under D-116.

reviewer_risks.risk: Tests 1-4's 'worse' readings use unadjusted intervals because Holm stopped at Test 3
reviewer_risks.answer: The three-way reading was pre-registered; Tests 1, 2 and 4's upper ends lie 13.75 to 20 points beyond the margin, Test 3's 2.2 points; run a multiplicity-corrected sensitivity with the correction fixed in advance (E-19); Test 3 already reads inconclusive in two views, which the paper shows.

reviewer_risks.risk: The marking rule was changed after seeing Sonnet's replies, and the change helped Sonnet
reviewer_risks.answer: Deviation 2 was declared before any main-run data, applies to every model, and both rules are reported; Test 5 holds under both; Test 3 is the reading that changes; Tests 1, 2 and 4 are unchanged.

reviewer_risks.risk: Deviation 1 (24 to 6 steps) could have created the negative vote result
reviewer_risks.answer: At 24 steps Haiku-medium scored near zero against Opus-medium's 96% and 88%; the move was ruled blind to Pilot 1's Opus and Sonnet results and N was picked by a Haiku-only rule with the length sweep's Opus and Sonnet answers sealed.

reviewer_risks.risk: Equal-money tests answer a different question from a buyer's 'cheapest route to a target accuracy', and k does not transfer
reviewer_risks.answer: Say so in the Introduction; show how k depends on price ratio, effort, shape and length; give the cost ratio per length; offer a labelled post hoc re-pricing table and a cost-for-target table if you agree (F-11).

reviewer_risks.risk: Small samples and wide intervals
reviewer_risks.answer: Give interval widths; power was simulated and locked before each study's data; say what each check could and could not detect; never order overlapping effort points.

reviewer_risks.risk: Puzzle sets differ in difficulty; cross-window comparisons in the top-up
reviewer_risks.answer: Keep every cross-study and cross-set comparison descriptive; take length comparisons from one study's sets; every cross-window comparison carries the same-model flag status, whose interval cannot rule out 8-10-point shifts; E2 against C13 is the same-window comparison.

reviewer_risks.risk: Effort labels are not a common unit across models; effort, tokens and token limits are confounded
reviewer_risks.answer: Define effort as the API's value; compare models by dollars and, descriptively, by measured tokens; never 'accuracy follows tokens, not the label'.

reviewer_risks.risk: Analysis code and reporting definitions were written after lock 3
reviewer_risks.answer: The driver was publicly stamped after collection and before any result was opened; the definitions were approved before results; all post-lock code and definitions are listed in the appendix; tier labels say where each item was fixed.

reviewer_risks.risk: Reproducibility: raw records not yet released; some run commits exist only on unmerged branches
reviewer_risks.answer: Release the call records and compact tables with hashes that agree with the public stamps; add a commit table and tool versions; merge and tag (needs your yes); venue and licence are your rulings.

reviewer_risks.risk: The Haiku picker chose reply 1 in 81 of 160 puzzles
reviewer_risks.answer: Position effects were not studied, and the paper says so; add the free 'take reply 1' baseline, accuracy by picked position and plurality agreement.

reviewer_risks.risk: B2's vote cost more than Opus-medium on chains (1.091)
reviewer_risks.answer: B2 always travels with its per-shape costs; the free analysis gives each shape's own equal-money k (5 on chains, 8 on pieces) with paired intervals.

reviewer_risks.risk: A claim title overstates a post hoc, one-family, one-cheap-model lesson; the judge question looks dodged
reviewer_risks.answer: Scope in the subtitle; no 'pre-registered' or 'equal-money' beside the claim; the abstract names Haiku 5.5 first; the judge question is stated as planned, left out before Study 1 (D-44) and open.

reviewer_risks.risk: Step voting is scored from correct inputs (an apparent oracle) and was far cheaper than Opus-medium
reviewer_risks.answer: Correct-input scoring equals the chance that a chain of independent step calls gets every step right; Test 4 is a cheap decomposition baseline, not an equal-money result; an E3 given Opus-medium's budget could not be rebuilt offline.

reviewer_risks.risk: The locked texts and stamped result files use the word 'matches'
reviewer_risks.answer: One Method sentence (F-15); stamped labels mapped in the data README; locked text quoted only as marked quotations.

reviewer_risks.risk: Test 2's result was forecast before the run; prompt-wording sensitivity; Batch versus real time; exposed puzzles; thinking-off floor
reviewer_risks.answer: Disclose the forecast (Test 2 only); report the +8.75-point rewording shift with its interval and small format share; say 'measured in Batch' (real-time subsets tiny, mixed directions); the exposed-base sensitivity gives the same B1-B3 readings; none of the 112 well-formed 16-step thinking-off chain replies was right.

plan.paid_run_verdict: No paid run. All four parts agree: every claim rests on the locked files, and nothing a paid run could buy changes any test result (D-116). The gaps the reviews name are stated as limits: no max-effort latency; the Haiku-max vote tested only at 16 steps (free analysis 2 adds descriptive curves at 6 and 12); in Study 1b, Sonnet and Opus-low only at 6 steps (the length sweep has Sonnet-medium at 12 and 16). If you still want one (F-14), the only option that removes a practitioner-facing limit is the max-effort latency check (about $7.84 at list by our arithmetic; it would need a spec, a lock, a trial round, Edith's clearance, a spend-log row and your go before the credit expires 2026-10-19 UTC, and a ruling because D-94(5) dropped the time axis). A 24-step run or Sonnet-high/Opus-low at 16 steps would each add one descriptive point across run windows. Recommendation: no paid run; spend the days on the free analyses from the top of the ranked list.

plan.summary_for_user:
How much more time: putting the four parts together into one plan is done (this step). One short step is left in this run: a final check of the plan, after which Jarvis files it. I can't see a clock from here, but it is a single checking pass, much smaller than the steps already finished. Nothing waits on money or on the credit deadline, because no paid run is needed.

What we do after that, in order:
1. Edith settles 27 fact and label questions. Most are about wording and labels; none can change a test result.
2. You choose 14 framing items, each with a recommended merged option: what the paper leads with, how frankly to say the tests never tried raising Haiku's effort, Test 3 in the abstract, how to frame Test 5, the power forecast, the title, the abstract sentences, the cheap-judge question, a buying-guide table, cost per 10,000 puzzles, how much to stress error ratios, any paid run (recommended: none), one sentence on the word 'matches', and what to call B3. Two items you left to the team are decided: the sentence to remember ('effort first, then voting', always labelled as our reading, not a test) and how much of the journey goes in the main text.
3. Free extra analyses on data we already have, no API money. The top ones: effort against more tries on the same puzzles at the same cost; Haiku-max vote curves at 6 and 12 steps; intervals for every vote size at 16 steps.
4. Karen turns the 129 claims into the claims ledger, and Friday builds the 41 tables and figures by script.
5. Then the writing, one section at a time: Method, Results, Discussion, then Introduction and abstract. Vision drafts each section, Edith checks it, you approve it.

Where the two reviews agreed: the numbers and the main findings. At medium effort, cheap Haiku votes fell short of one Opus answer. A small vote of max-effort Haiku tries was no worse than Opus by more than 5 points, at about Opus's price. They also agreed on the list of free analyses and that no paid run is needed.

Where they differed: Fable, which read blind, stated several results more strongly than the files allow. It called the two inconclusive single-try tests 'measurably worse', said 'a seventh of the price', made repeated wrong answers the cause of the vote plateau, and called the picker 'position-biased'. The files and the locked plan side with Opus's careful wording. On the story, Fable said the pre-registered tests asked a narrower question than the brief: they never tried raising the cheap model's effort. Opus told it as a surprise. The plan keeps the surprise and also says Fable's point plainly, in one paragraph.

What Fable found that Opus missed: the forecast made before the run that Test 2 would come out as it did; that Sonnet ran one level below its default effort, while at its default (on other puzzles) it scored 97.5 at under half Opus-low's price; lower accuracy in the small real-time check; that the Opus side of the fairness check was nearly empty; the ceiling on what any picker choosing among 8 medium-effort answers could reach; the chain-versus-pieces reference line on the length curve; and several analyses we can run free on existing data.

What Opus found that Fable missed: Opus knew the rulings Fable could not see, so it got the labels and caveats right. Test 3 does not hold in every view. Opus-high missed 3 times, not once. The 16-step thinking-off result is not mostly a format failure. Neither review cited your ruling that dropped the cheap-judge study; the plan now does. Both made one shared mistake, saying Sonnet ran only at 6 steps (true only inside Study 1b); it is fixed.

Fixes made while assembling: I re-read the code to confirm that the length-curve reference line uses pieces only. I rewrote a few phrases that hid a banned word inside compounds like 'budget-matched'. I corrected one count against the spend log (the early digit-puzzle run had 3 refusals in 9 calls, not 2). I sent two places where the parts disagreed to Edith: a size comparison for the rewording check and a latency estimate.

corrections.corrected_text: Main message (our reading across both studies, not a test; each part keeps its own tier; the studies differ in puzzle sets, lengths and days, and no drift check links them): effort first, then voting. On one synthetic family of exact multi-step puzzles, raising Haiku 5.5's effort to max helped far more than any multi-call design tried at medium effort. At no more than Opus-medium's price, medium-effort Haiku votes were worse than one Opus-medium answer by more than the 10-point margin (Tests 1-2, confirmatory; pre-registered three-way readings of unadjusted intervals, not Holm-declared). So was step voting, at about 1/11 of the cost (Test 4, same reading). The Haiku team stayed 27.5-43.75 points below Opus-medium. The Haiku picker's 62.5 / 67.5 sat about 33 points below Opus-medium's 96.25 / 100 (both exploratory and across run windows, same-model flag not fired; the picker gap is arithmetic, with no interval). We could not show that a single Haiku-max try is within 5 points of Opus-medium (B1 at 16 steps, B3 at 6 steps; confirmatory, inconclusive at the primary margin). Its error rate was 3.4 and 6.8 times Opus-medium's, at about 1/6 (16 steps) and 1/10 (6 steps) of the cost per answer (k measured). At the secondary 10-point margin it was no worse than Opus-medium by more than 10 points. At 16 steps, the expected accuracy of a 6-try Haiku-max vote was no worse than one Opus-medium answer by more than 5 points (B2, confirmatory, declared under Holm), at about its price (0.894 pooled; 1.091 on chains, 0.733 on pieces).

On 6-step puzzles, at no more than Opus-medium's price, a Haiku-medium vote was worse than one Opus-medium answer by more than 10 points (Tests 1-2, confirmatory; pre-registered three-way reading of the unadjusted 95% interval, not Holm-declared). On fresh 16-step puzzles, the expected accuracy of a vote of 6 Haiku-max tries (estimated from 10 tries per puzzle) was no worse than one Opus-medium answer by more than 5 points (d +0.63, 95% interval -1.15 to +2.44; Test B2, confirmatory, declared under Holm), at about Opus-medium's price per answer (0.894 of it pooled over shapes; 1.091 on chains, 0.733 on pieces). A single Haiku-max try, at about 1/10 (6 steps) to 1/6 (16 steps) of Opus-medium's cost per answer (k measured), was no worse than one Opus-medium answer by more than 10 points (the secondary margin), but we could not show it within 5 points (B1, B3; confirmatory, inconclusive at the 5-point primary margin). Its error rate was 3.4 times Opus-medium's at 16 steps (95% interval 1.8 to 10.1) and 6.8 times at 6 steps (1.7 to unbounded).

applied_corrections.corrected_text: Haiku with thinking off (exploratory arm; medium effort with thinking disabled) scored 22.0 [16.97, 27.31] on chains and 23.5 [18.8, 28.6] on pieces, against Haiku-medium's 43.72 / 51.0, and saved about 19% / 12.5% of the cost per puzzle. On chains, 18.3% of its replies also failed the format (the format flag fires); scored on the final answer alone, it reached 28.0 instead of the official 22.0. applied_corrections.corrected_text: Counts only, no test. On chains, the team's aggregator changed 42 of 80 final answers, turning 15 right helper chains wrong and 7 wrong ones right (the 42 include 2 unreadable aggregator replies and 1 puzzle where the helpers had no result, both counted as differing by the pre-stated rule). On pieces it changed 34, turning 9 right ones wrong and 18 wrong ones right. By our arithmetic, the helpers' own result would have been right on about 50 of 80 chains (62.5%) and 49 of 80 pieces (61.25%). On pieces, about half of the team's 21.25-point lead over C13 came with the aggregator's net changes (helpers alone about 61.25 against C13's 51.25). applied_corrections.corrected_text: Our data echo known effects without testing them (our reading, not a test): on the 16 chain puzzles where a single Haiku-medium try was right less than 10% of the time, a 40-try vote scored 0.
